Thank you to my team mate Anna, all participants, Kaggle Admin, Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard who realized this exciting competition. I would like to briefly share our 5th place solution.
Problem settings
The most difficult problem in this competition seems to be that there are both seen and unseen drugs in the test set. This makes construction of the reliable validation difficult.
Validation strategies and their properties
In this competition, there are mainly two types of validation strategies used. One is traditional MultilabelStratifiedKFold, and the other is MultilabelStratifiedGroupKFold which is a group awared one (aka Chris's method). Seeing predictions by models based on these schemes, MultilabelStratifiedKFold seems to give more confident predictions for seen drugs, whereas MultilabelStratifiedGroupKFold gives more balanced and robust predictions which are supposed to be suitable for unseen drugs. I thought that both are useful in different ways.
Our approach
The setting where both seen and unseen labels are observed in the test set is similar to that in
Bengali.AI Handwritten Grapheme Classification
. So we decided to discriminate seen and unseen drugs by metric learning (L2 Softmax -> cosine similarity) and then blended models trained on each validation scheme based on the similarity. This separation of seen/unseen seems to be possible to some extent as shown in the figure below. This approach does not require something like pseudo-labelling & retraining. Simple forward processing is enough.
Features
Raw cell and genes
PCA
rankGauss
PolynominalFeatures
Simple statistics like mean, min, max, skew, kurt, (X_train>9).sum(axis=1)
etc.
Models
ResNet-like shallow NN
TabNet
For especially models for unseen drugs, we used simple networks.
Reconstruction of drug_id [Updated]
From the very beginning of the competition, I was validating my models based on a method nearly equivalent to Chris CV.  For this purpose, I reconstructed drug_id by heuristic methods, including clustering and many manual adjustments. The official drug_id was published in the later stages of the competition, but many participants may have already overfitted. Once anyone has produced a good Public LB score, it's very hard to suspect that it's overfitting. The temptation and pleasure of running up LB is so intense.
Below are the CV results from both methods for the same model. My method worked almost as well as the Chris CV. I switched to Chris CV at the end of the competition because it performed a bit better. I think that Chris CV was good at handling drug_id with lots of observations and was similar to the actual splits.

Thank you to the LISH Competition Organizers, the Kaggle Team, and everyone who shared notebooks and contributed to the discussions.
TL;DR: Our final submission was a simple weighted average of an MLP, TabNet, and ResNet model.
Dimensionality Reduction
We decided to do dimensionality reduction on the full test set. This meant we had to retrain the models when the private test set became available and so we couldn't do an inference-only submission. We used a mix of PCA, SVD, and ICA depending on the model.
Early Stopping for Each Target
All of our models used early stopping for each target. The idea was to keep track of the best epoch for each of the targets separately. For example, this plot shows the log loss on a few of the targets.
If we had used a single epoch's weights for every target, we would have overfit some targets and underfit others.
Validation
We tried a lot of variants of CV, but in the end, we went with MultilabelStratifiedKFold and did not use
train_drug.csv
. Our CV-LB alignment was still shaky and there was clearly a point at which further CV improvement degraded LB.
@Chris Deotte's
smart
CV scheme
was promising, but it did not solve this entirely for us.  Our LB scores with the smart CV scheme were a bit worse than with MultilabelStratifiedKFold, similar to what other teams noticed.
Final Blend
Our final submission was a simple weighted average of
0.5*mlp + 0.3*tabnet + 0.2*resnet
. We did not use the public LB to tune these weights, and that probably helped prevent some overfitting.

A big thank you to the Laboratory for Innovation Science at Harvard and to the Kaggle team for hosting this competition, as well as to all other participants who created such a friendly and yet challenging competitive environment! This was my first DS competition and I learned a lot from you.
From multilabel to multiclass
The main idea behind my solution was reframing the multilabel prediction problem as multiclass classification to leverage correlations between targets. Even though there were originally 206 binary targets, the training dataset contained only 328 distinct combinations of them. I gave each a class label from 0 to 327, using it as target variable instead. The correspondence between class labels and original targets was stored in a 328x206 matrix.
Then I set up NN models with a softmax activation in the last layer, yielding probability matrices of shape (batch_size x 328) and optimizing for categorical cross-entropy. To retrieve predictions for the 206 original targets, I multiplied the NN output by the 328x206 matrix.
While in theory this "dual" approach is more limited due to the fact that it is impossible to give perfect predictions for a new drug with MoA combinations not previously seen among the 328 classes, in practice these individual models still had decent performance by themselves (best public/private LB scores were 0.01849/0.1633 with NNs and 0.01830/0.01623 with Tabnet).
However, their biggest power came when blending with other models, because this reframing significantly lowered the prediction correlations, as it detects different signals from the training data.
Final solution
My final solution was a simple average (no weighting) of four models: two Tabnets and two NNs (one multiclass and one multilabel for each architecture). Nothing remarkable about the feature engineering pipeline: I used QuantileTransformer, PCA and row-based statistics as it was done in several public notebooks.
The details of my top selected submission can be seen below (0.01811/0.01603 LB), but I achieved similar private scores of 0.01603 and 0.01604 with other model combinations.

Summary
Denoising Autoencoder
I used normal denoising autoencoder instead of the swapping method, and I concatenated it with the original features. It improved the public test socre from 0.01842 to 0.01834 but CV was not improved.
Weighted Loss
I used weighted loss which weights targets that only occur few times in the train data (I used 40).

title: Google Research Football with Manchester City F.C.: Train agents to master the worlds most popular sport
introduction:
== Description ===
Manchester City F.C. and Google Research are proud to present AI football competition using the
Google Research Football Environment
.
A word from Manchester City F.C.
Brian Prestidge, Director of Data Insights & Decision Technology at City Football Group, the owners of Manchester City F.C., sets out the challenge. “Football is a tough environment to perform in and an even tougher environment to learn in. Learning is all about harnessing failure, but failure in football is seldom accepted. Working with Google Research’s physics based football environment provides us with a new place to learn through simulation and offers us the capabilities to test tactical concepts and refine principles so that they are strong enough for a coach to stake their career on.”
“We are therefore very pleased to be working with Google’s research team in creating this competition and are looking forward to the opportunity to support some of the most creative and successful competitors through funding and exclusive prizes. We hope to establish ongoing collaboration with the winners beyond this competition, and that it will provide us all with the platform to explore and establish fundamental principles of football tactics, thus improving our ability to perform and be successful on the pitch.”
Greg Swimer, Chief Technology Officer at City Football Group added "Technologies such as Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence have huge future potential to enhance the understanding and enjoyment of football for players, coaches and fans.  We are delighted to be collaborating with Google's research team to help broaden the knowledge, talent, and innovation working in this exciting and transformational area".
The Google Research football environment competition
The world gets a kick out of football (soccer in the United States). As the most popular sport on the planet, millions of fans enjoy watching Sergio Agüero, Raheem Sterling, and Kevin de Bruyne on the field. Football video games are less lively, but still immensely popular, and we wonder if AI agents would be able to play those properly.
Researchers want to explore AI agents' ability to play in complex settings like football. The sport requires a balance of short-term control, learned concepts such as passing, and high-level strategy, which can be difficult to teach agents. A current environment exists to train and test agents, but other solutions may offer better results.
The teams at Google Research aspire to make discoveries that impact everyone. Essential to their approach is sharing research and tools to fuel progress in the field. Together with Manchester City F.C., Google Research has put forth this competition to get help in reaching their
goal
.
In this competition, you’ll create AI agents that can play football. Teams compete in “steps,” where agents react to a game state. Each agent in an 11 vs 11 game controls a single active player and takes actions to improve their team’s situation. As with a typical football game, you want your team to score more than the other side. You can optionally see your efforts rendered in a physics-based 3D football simulation.
If controlling 11 football players with code sounds difficult, don't be discouraged! You only need to control one player at a time (the one with the ball on offense, or the one closest to the ball on defense) and your code gets to pick from 1 of 19 possible actions. We have prepared a
getting started
example to show you how simple a basic strategy can be. Before implementing your own strategy, however, you might want to learn more about
the Google Research football environment
, especially
observations provided to you by the environment and available actions
. You can also
play the game yourself
on your computer locally to get better understanding of the environment's dynamics and explore different scenarios.
If successful, you'll help researchers explore the ability of AI agents to play in complex settings. This could offer new insights into the strategies of the world's most-watched sport. Additionally, this research could pave the way for a new generation of AI agents that can be trained to learn complex skills.

== Evaluation ===
Each day, your team is able to submit up to 5 agents (bots) to the competition. Each submission will play episodes (games) against other bots on the ladder that have a similar skill rating. Over time, skill ratings will go up with wins or down with losses. Every bot submitted will continue to play games until the end of the competition. On the leaderboard only your best scoring bot will be shown, but you can track the progress of all of your submissions on your Submissions page.
Each Submission has an estimated Skill Rating which is modeled by a Gaussian N(μ,σ2) where μ is the estimated skill and σ represents our uncertainty of that estimate which will decrease over time.
When you upload a Submission, we first play a Validation Episode where that Submission plays against a copy of itself to make sure it works properly. If the Episode fails, the Submission is marked as Error. Otherwise, we initialize the Submission with μ0=600 and it joins the pool of All Submissions for ongoing evaluation.
We repeatedly run Episodes from the pool of All Submissions and try to pick Submissions with similar ratings for fair matches. We aim to run ~8 Episodes a day per Submission with an additional slight rate increase for the newest-submitted Episodes to give you feedback faster.
After an Episode finishes, we'll update the Rating estimate of both agents in that Episode. If one agent won, we'll increase its μ and decrease its opponent's μ -- if the result was a draw, then we'll move the two μ values closer towards their mean. The updates will have magnitude relative to the deviation from the expected result based on the previous μ values, and also relative to each Submission's uncertainty σ. We also reduce the σ terms relative to the amount of information gained by the result. The score by which your bot wins or loses an Episode does not affect the skill rating updates.
At the submission deadline, additional submissions will be locked. One additional week will be allotted to continue to run games. At the conclusion of this week, the leaderboard is final.

solutions.1st place:
It is a wonderful journey and we learned  a lot from this competition. First of all, let's give all our thanks and respects to the competition holders: Kaggle team, Manchester City and Google research.  I believe your work including the google-football environment and the this competition will inspire the research of multi-agent reinforcement learning, and I look forward to more chanllenging football competitions in the future.
We also want to say thanks to other teams in this competition, especially
SaltyFish
，
Raw Beast
and
kangaroo
.  Your are respectable opponents and we learned and improved a lot by watching games from your agents.
We totally build our agents using  reinforcement learning and selfplay. Now let's introduce how we made it.
1. Training framework
Our training framework is very similar to framwork desribed in
Deheng Ye, et al
; By   sacrificing part of real-time ability, this asynchronous archarchitecture gives us  big flexibility to use  and change computer resources during training.
2. Network Architecture
Our model consists of a few dense layers (256 dim each) and a LSTM block(32 steps, 256 hidden size).  PPO from
openai baseline
is adjusted to our framework for the training. Learning rate is 1e-4 and is fixed. Adam optimizer is used for paramater update.
SMM feature and CNN block were tested at the very early stage, but soon abandonded due to low traning speed and high memory consumption. Fast adaptation and iteration play more important role in our solution.
To decrease variance of value estimation, we introduce multi-head value(MHV) (as is done in
Deheng Ye, et al 2020
). Rewards are decomposed to different heads, and accumulated with various discount factors. Idea behind is that some events are only highly correlated with recent actions, such as intercepts, offsides and slides, while some events are achieved by sequential decisions on a longer horizon, like goal.
The total value estimation is then the weighted sum of the head value estimates:
3. Feature Engineering
We extend the standard 115 dim vectors with some more features :
relative pose(position, direction) among teammates and opponents
relative pose between active player and ball
offside flag to mark potential offside teammates
sticky actions/card/tried factor status
Efficiency Gain：
about 30% training speedup.
Performance Gain：
No ablation study on performance though, but it is reasonable to believe more features should help the agent make better decisions.
4. Reward shaping
Since the scoring rewrad is too sparse, we designed serveral dense rewards to speed up the training and adjust agent play style. During the designing of reward, we thought making it
zero-sum
is very important for self-play.
intercept & outside & offside: zero-sum, +0.2 for getting possession, -0.2 for losing possession.
slide: zero-sum, +0.2 for our successful slide, -0.2 for opponent successful slide. We found slide is useful for defence, so we added this reward during early training.
hold ball: zero-sum, +0.001 if team holds the ball('ball_owned_team' = 0), -0.001 if opponent holds the ball('ball_owned_team' = 1).
pass: +0.1 for each pass before a goal. This reward is added to scroing reward, because we just want to encourage passing which is helpful for the goal.
Above are general rewards that we used. We also designed some specialized rewards to increase diversity, e.g., reward that encourges agent attacks in middle way (most of our other models prefer attack from the wings).
Besides handcrafted reward shaping, we also utilized GAIL(
Jonathan Ho et al
) to learn from other teams. For example, when we first matched kangaroo, their 'counter attack' style(take ball and go backwards -> pass to golie -> golie high pass to front court) really impressed us. We found it was hard to write a reward to imitate them, so we used GAIL to learn from their replays. Models trained with GAIL were then played as fixed opponents in furthering training, which can enhance robustness of our models.
5. Opponent pool
Although our base models have led the LB from the beginning, and only need to upload models with larger traing epoch to keep advantage from time to time, we still have concerns that naive selfplay converges to local optimum and does not generalize well. To add diversity and robustness to our strategy, League training similiar to that in
Vinyals et al. 2019
is adopted. Models with distinct preferences are created independently by reward shaping or learning from demonstrations in the first stage, and further evolve simoutanously by combating with each other. A final model is then trained, with the aim to beat all league. Typical styles include:
counter-attack favoured: inspired by
kangoroo
, submission id 18338177,
demo episode
short pass favoured: inspired by
SaltyFish
, not uploaded
holding ball favoured: very interesting one, submission id 18336333,
demo episode
.
Since models from different league also improve in themselves, these sub-optimal stratagies exhibit competative skills as well and achieve high elo. Till 8th Dec, kaggle elo for the 1st and the 3rd style are 1705 and 1706 respectively. Internal LB indicates that our final model taking all styles as opponents can get extra 100 elo in advance, compared to our silver candidate.
6. Evaluation
Due to the limited play frequency of LB, it usually took 2~3 days to see the real rank of a newly uploaded model. To efficiently evaluate our models, we maintained a model pool and set up a local LB. Each time a new model is trained, it will be added to the model pool and play against with each other. The score of models were calculated accoriding to the standard ELO algorithm. Although the ELO result is not fully transitive (models with lower score may beat those with higher score), the rank of our local LB was highly correlated with the public LB.
solutions.2nd place:
It has been a great pleasure to join this football competition on Kaggle! We thank the
Kaggle team
,
Manchester City
, and
Google research
for the effort of making this happen! It seems that the gfootball team launched this competition in early 2020 and was intended to hold the final on ICML. Unfortunately, it is a tough year…… and we hope everybody is okay. Back to the competition, we also wanna thank all the participants, and it is you guys that make this competition wonderful and exciting! Special thanks to
Wekick
, your agents are really impressive and we also learned a lot from you.
Summary
Generally speaking, we train our agents through
reinforcement learning
by integrating
PVE
and
Selfplay
. Under
limited computation resources
, it is hard for the agents to learn from scratch (selfplay) in such a difficult environment (long-time horizon and sparse reward). By first training against the easy bot (difficulty_level = 0.05) and then the hard bot (difficulty_level = 1.0) until convergence, our agents get some clue on offense (e.g., dribbling the ball from backcourt to frontcourt, shooting skill). The selfplay phase then enables the agents to learn defense skills and further enhances the offense skill by learning passing skills. Let's get into some details.
Algorithm
We use distributed IMPALA implemented in our framework
RLEase
. RLEase is a highly efficient reinforcement learning based library developed by
Netease Fuxi Lab
, which both incorporates state-of-the-art algorithms (such as IMPALA, APEX-rainbow, PPO, VDN, QMIX, etc.) and supports distributed training, models' auto testing, imitation learning and offers an easy API to incorporate new game environments. The framework looks like this:
Feature
We first tried the simple115 wrapper that is mostly based on absolute values, which turned out to be lacking generalization capabilities. Then we extended it to the multi-head vector input by adding relative information and grouping related features into one head. Besides,
surgery
is also used to add extra features since training from the very beginning is both costly and not feasible under limited resources, just like what
OpenAI Five
did. The figure below shows what the multi-head vector inputs look like, where the blue columns represent the original input and the red columns and texts represent the surgery part.
Network
We use several fully-connected layers. See Figure below:
Action
We use different action sets for the algorithm in different 'ball_owned_team' modes (i.e., 0, 1, and -1). The main purpose is to ignore the unnecessary actions and reduce the exploration space. For example, when one player of our team has the ball, there is no need to choose the SLIDING action. For each 'ball_owned_team' mode, we simply generate a corresponding legal/illegal mask vector to indicate which of the 19 actions can be or cannot be taken. The output of the policy network (i.e., the probability of taking each action) will be updated according to the mask vector. We list the illegal actions in each 'ball_owned_team' mode as follows:
ball_owned_team
= 0: SLIDING
ball_owned_team
= 1: LONG_PASS, HIGH_PASS, SHORT_PASS, SHOT, DRIBBLE, STOP_DRIBBLE
ball_owned_team
= -1: LONG_PASS, HIGH_PASS, SHORT_PASS, SHOT, DRIBBLE, STOP_DRIBBLE, SLIDING
Although such a trick can accelerate learning by avoiding unnecessary actions, it also makes our algorithm unable to learn some strong policies. For example, in the last few weeks of this competition, we found that one entry of WeKick had learned the skill of passing the ball between players without stopping the ball. When the ball was flying from the passer to the receiver, the receiver had already chosen the most appropriate position and facing direction for performing the next pass. Once the ball got very close to the receiver (we found that the `ball_owned_team' at that time was still -1), the ball would be passed to the next receiver. This kind of ball-passing tactic really impressed us and we realized that our model cannot pass the ball in the same way. Therefore, in the last week, we trained another model without legal action masks. This no-legal-action model actually has the highest score (1597.5) among all our submitted models at the end of the extra evaluation week. Interestingly, the highest score achieved by our legal-action models is 1597.0. The no-legal-action model successfully learned the ball-passing skill, though not as skillful as WeKick. We expect it will perform better if there are another extra week and more computation resources for training…
Reward
For the PVE training, we use the scoring reward and checkpoint reward. The latter is also provided by the gfootball environment (please refer to the gfootball paper). We found that using the checkpoint rewards is really helpful in the early training stage because such rewards are the most straightforward for encouraging the player to take the ball from the backcourt to the frontcourt and make a goal. At the end of the PVE training phase, our model can beat the hard bot (difficulty_level = 1.0) with a goal difference higher than 10. However, the disadvantage of the checkpoint rewards is that the behavior of the player output by the model is always dribbling the ball (maybe with sprint). In fact, the PVE-trained model is not a strong model and the learned policy is very easy to exploit. The only purpose of using the checkpoint rewards is to let our agent get some clue on the offense.
For selfplay training, we use the scoring reward and abandon checkpoint reward to let our model learn more sophisticated behaviors. Note that the model is based on the PVE-trained model, which is good at dribbling, shooting, and scoring. Therefore, the reward signals are not that sparse in selfplay.
We also tried different shaping rewards in order to learn models with different behavior styles, such as using ball possession rewards (e.g., 0.1 for getting the ball and -0.1 for losing the ball possession) to encourage tighter defense and using ball passing rewards (e.g., 0.01 for a successful pass and -0.01 for an unsuccessful one) to get a pass-favored policy. The positive result is that with different shaping rewards, the behavior styles learned by the models are quite different. For example, with the ball passing rewards, the number of passes executed and the number of passes completed of the corresponding model in a match is at least two times higher than those of the other models. However, none of the shaping rewards adopted were able to train very strong models. The reasons are two-fold. Firstly, setting an appropriate value for each type of reward is a difficult problem and needs tedious tuning. Secondly, our shaping rewards actually are not directly related to the goal of scoring, which is also pointed out by the
Raw Beast
team.
Resource
During the first several months before the Kaggle competition, we only have 80 CPU cores and it takes ages to get the model to work (around 190k episodes per week). The training scale is similar to that of
liveinparis
) and after training for two weeks, the model can reach up to 1400+ on the previous leaderboard before Kaggle. For the Kaggle competition, we use 1000 CPU cores for each experiment (20k+ fps in our framework) and a maximum of 2500 CPU cores in the last two weeks (1000 for non-legal action masks training, 1000 for adding pre-16 steps action surgery training, and 500 for curriculum training and imitation learning). In addition, GPUs are not necessary since we use vectors as inputs.
Other methods we tried:
ELO-based Opponent Selection: We tried to select the opponent by using the Elo rank during selfplay, which turns out to be similar to the performance of selecting the newest opponent with a certain ratio (70%) in this football environment.
Curriculum Learning and Imitation Learning：We also used curriculum learning to help our agents to learn useful skills such as shooting from the middle of the field during freekick (see the gif bellow). Besides, we also cloned the behavior of Wekick and put the model in our opponent pools.
https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/v2-ead94061921f49028929cc30cdf10afc_r.gif
Action Semantics Network: We tried the action semantics network (ASN), which is proposed in an ICLR2020 paper (
https://openreview.net/forum?id=ryg48p4tPH)
. The motivation of using ASN is that in this football scenario, different actions of a player may require differnt observations. For example, for applying the SLIDING action, a player should pay more attention to the ball and the player controlling the ball. And for applying the SHOT action, the player should take the ball, the opponent goalkeeper, maybe the opponent players nearby as well into consideration. However, our computation resources are limited and this model is still in the training process.
Behavior Tree as Macro Action: We extended the action space size from 19 to 20 by adding a new action 'behavior tree' and trained a new model. This new action means to get the behavior of the player controlled according to a behavior-tree AI. You can simply treat a behavior-tree AI as a rule-based AI. Most importantly, such a behavior-tree AI is a python version of the
eliza_controller
in the internal C++ code of the gfootball_engine, namely the internal bot provided by the environment. The motivation for utilizing the internal bot is that such a bot is good at ball passing and ball controlling. We believe that a stronger model can be obtained if it has the ball passing and ball controlling skills of the internal bot. However, this model is still in the training process under limited resources.
Graph Neural Networks: We also tried the graph neural networks (such as GCN and GAT) to extract features. The features of the players are designed as a fully connected graph, where we represent the players' information with the graph's nodes and relations between players with edges. However, this model is still being trained under limited resources.

solutions.3rd place:
This has been fun! A big thank you to the Kaggle team, Manchester City and Google research for making the challenge an incredible learning experience. Your support has been excellent throughout the entire period. Simulation competitions give an extra dimension to Kaggle and we were very excited to participate in the first competition that really required reinforcement learning (RL) to excel.
We would like to thank the teams WeKick and SaltyFish for raising the bar for all of us. Your agents are truly impressive and we can’t wait to find out how you approached the exploration problem. Yegor
@yegorbiryukov
did another great job at building a conceptually simple but highly effective rule based agent which served as an excellent sparring partner for our initial RL agents.
During the past two months we tried hard to master the world’s most popular sport. Let us tell you about our journey that touched on rule based strategies, behavior cloning of top submissions and deep reinforcement learning.
We started this competition with an open mind after both having independently topped the two previous Simulations competitions with a rule-based approach (
@dott1718
in
ConnectX
and
@tvdwiele
in
Halite
). Initially, we tried out a rule-based approach to get familiar with the game but it quickly became clear that this was not going to scale, so we moved to the RL setup described next.
Summary of the final strategy
Our final approach is very similar to the effort of the
AlphaStar publication
(see
nature link
- pseudocode.zip for the implementation details).
We initially train a network using supervised learning to predict the action probabilities of one or more submission ids, given the current state. In our setup, this can already lead to a relatively strong agent (around the 20th place on the leaderboard).
The network from the behavior cloning is then used as the starting point for the actor component of our actor-critic RL approach. During RL, we add a Kullback-Leibler (KL) distribution loss to the original result of the cloning to make sure we don’t completely forget about the policy of the original submissions. Adding the KL stabilizes learning and helps to add diversity to our agents pool, since the resulting RL agents are constrained not to move too far away from the starting point in policy space. We also experimented with an ongoing cloning loss which worked similarly to the KL to the clone.
When learning slows down, we pick the point it ends up with as the starting point for the next round and train it with a KL to that new reference policy.
In our experiments, just like in the AlphaStar effort, it turned out that the strength of the cloned agent correlated highly with the strength of the agent after RL.
Behavior cloning
We train the cloning policy with the cross-entropy loss of the actions that were selected by the target submissions. We also add an entropy bonus to the loss.
The performance of the cloning gets better as it is fed more data. Assuming that the strategy is
symmetric about the x-axis
, data augmentation can double the amount of data. We used this type of data augmentation for some runs and it typically helped. But it was not always the case, as many agents had clearly asymmetrical behavior, counting also the agents we produced with RL.
Combining different submissions is less obvious since it only really makes sense to combine similar strategies. To decide what submissions are similar, we looked at marginal action frequencies of the agents based on replays of their games and MDS embeddings of action distribution distances of single-submission clones:
Due to limited data available for cloning an agent's behavior, we tried simple ways of transfer learning and experienced a significant boost of the clone performance. In the first approach, the torso of the network was trained to be able to predict the action probabilities of 20 different submissions after concatenating the torso outputs with a one-hot encoding of the submission id. That way, the network is forced to learn generic features which then in turn allows for faster learning in subsequent cloning efforts. Another approach is to pre-train the model on a larger set of other submissions and continue training the network on the data from the target submission.
Feature engineering
We add a couple of features to the game state to make the observations more Markovian. Some actions, including passing, can take several steps before they are executed. In order to make the agent aware of such actions, we add an encoding of the time since the last pass, shot and sliding.
Additionally, we add several features to reduce the variance during RL:
Features related to the opponent controlled player - only provided to the value network since this information is not readily available at inference time
Offside boolean flag for all friendly players. This summarizes the relevant past to know if a player will be penalized with a free kick upon controlling the ball due to the offside rule. That way, the value network can better assess the value of a state, since it learns on unrolls of size 32/64 and we use temporal difference learning for credit assignment.
Network architecture
We tried several shapes of convolutional networks and made an attempt of using transformers, but quite quickly converged to convolutions-based architecture as a good balance between speed and size of the model. The model consists of blocks of dense layers, 1-D and 2-D convolutions across players, which are concatenated before the last set of dense layers.
“Active player block” with the features from the active player’s point of view: location, direction of movement and sticky actions.
“Opponents block” with the 1-D convolution over 11 opponents using their positions and velocities relative to the active player as features.
“Teammates block” with the same structure as for the opponents.
“Pairs block” with a 10x11 tensor containing location and velocity of each opponent relative to each teammate and a 2-D convolution over it with average pooling per teammate.
“Main opponent” with the features of the opponent closest to the ball using the same features.
“Game data” with the indicator of the team in possession, ball location and speed, game mode.
“Historical features” like time since last passing or shooting action
“Active opponent data” for value function only
Building a wider network didn’t bring much benefit and cost quite a lot of resources, but a deeper version was quite efficient and became our final choice. We adjusted the number of layers to get the most out of the network performance, while keeping the runtime and learning time low enough. According to the logs, our submissions take only 0.01-0.15 seconds per action, so we were safe from timeout risk.
Assessing the agents
One could have used the public leaderboard to assess the strength of the agents, but, even though it gives a good picture of how the agent behaves against the real opponents, this strategy has a major flaw. The variance of the LB scores is too high. For instance, we had 2 identical agents submitted with 1 day distance between them and after a week they had close to 90 points LB score difference.
In order to judge on the RL progress and to assess the performance of produced agents, we maintained and constantly updated a set of agents, with as diverse strategies as possible. This set included rule based agents we developed, publicly available agents, clones and RL agents. This way we maintained a more flexible and reliable internal LB, where we played enough games to lower the variance, and this way ensured the progress.
Core Reinforcement Learning
General setup
We implemented a custom version in PyTorch of the
IMPALA
architecture for the core RL logic: asynchronous acting and learning with an off-policy correction for the actor-critic agent. That allows us to be data efficient through the use of a replay buffer since acting is relatively slow compared to learning.
Figure from the IMPALA paper:
Environment
It was only two weeks before the deadline that we realized we were training on an old version of the environment (2.6) where passing was fundamentally broken. After upgrading to 2.8, our agent became a big fan of passing.
Reward
Initially, we used complex hand crafted rewards with a disjoint setup (1 RL agent per mode) where we had separate rewards for each of 4 game modes: distant from goal/close to goal attack/defense. This was a bad idea and I should have known (Tom in this paragraph). During my time at DeepMind, a common theme was that the solutions got better as the reward was simplified by making it a more straightforward mapping of the real objective (as long as there is at least some reward). When we moved to a straightforward single mode reward for scoring/conceding a goal, RL started working. It turns out that temporal difference learning actually works!
Acting
Half of the experience in our experiments comes from self-play. Self-play is nice because it always ensures a well matched opponent, is twice as data efficient as playing against other agents and allows for detecting the local blind spots in the current policy. The downside of only doing self-play is that it can lead to cycles.
The second half of the experience comes from playing against a pool of fixed opponents. In our experience, we got better results with a big (about 10) pool of diverse opponent strategies.
The combination of the two data modes made sure we saw few cycles in policy space and typically saw a reliable up going performance trend.
Towards the end of the competition, we experimented with a third data mode: leaderboard experience of our agents - this would allow the agent to become robust against the actual opponents it is matched with. This was added too late and did not end up making it to our best submissions.
Learning
The discount factor is set to 0.999 and we only use terminal rewards of -1, 0 (end of a half) or 1 for scoring or conceding a goal. The unrolls are set to 32 or 64 and we use a batch size of 1024 transitions. We use a similar loss as the one used in AlphaStar, except for the latent variable which we don’t have in our setup:
TD-lambda value loss (lambda 0.9)
IMPALA policy loss. Thank you FAIR and “Heiner the hero” in specific for providing
torchbeast
- this was key to get the IMPALA policy loss right.
UPGO policy loss
Entropy bonus
KL loss to the initial policy
Additionally, we add a trust-region style KL loss to make sure that the policy does not change too much during a learning iteration (single pass through the data of the replay buffer of 800,000 transitions). Adding this was important to stabilize learning, especially when training without a KL to the original policy.
We use a separate actor and critic architecture without any parameter sharing. The actor and critic parameters are optimized with different Adam optimizers and the learning rate of the critic was typically set to two times the learning rate of the actor. When starting from a clone, it was important not to start updating the actor until the critic was at least fairly decent. Otherwise, the agent would tend to greedily update the policy, especially when training without a KL to the original policy.
Debugging
Getting RL right is hard. Therefore we spent a lot of effort into developing adequate tools to inspect the learning dynamics. A video of the evolution of the policy and value function while learning is attached for the first 300 steps of a game of self-play.
YouTube network probabilities
Taking it further
We have reasons to believe that the limiting factor in learning progress is the actor data rate. The next step would be to distribute our data gathering across several machines, rather than using the current multi threading data collection which is limited by the number of cores on the learning machine.
Engineering setup to scale up our experiments
RL is resource greedy and needs hours and days of running to get a good lift in the performance, so getting all the pieces of code as efficient as possible is a must. But RL has even more moving parts to tweak in order to find the best setup: tons of hyperparameters of the NN fitting and the acting-learning routine, NN structure and input features, actor and critic initialization points, pool of the opponents. Therefore we needed an easy way to trigger multiple experiments across the machines at our disposal and the ability to oversee the progress to make necessary corrections. First step was to automate as many steps as possible, starting from setting up and installing the environment (which is not easy), and as we had to use machines with different setups and OS versions, we ended up running all the experiments in docker containers. The code base was relatively static, while experiment setups were constantly changing, therefore we synchronized the work through an s3 bucket: experiment configurations, execution progress and checkpoints, agents, replays.
Given the hardware limits and the necessity to tweak and tune the parameters, each experiment was running in a single container (actor and learner in separate threads), but the next step would have been to synchronize the experience buffer across multiple machines and take the learning to a larger scale.
Curated list of ideas we couldn’t get to work
Train with an architecture that shares the torso between the actor and the critic.
Transformer-based network architecture
Add summary of the recent past as additional inputs (beyond the features mentioned above). Example: summarize the ball trajectory to be better able to project where the ball will end up.
Start from a mixture distribution of different initial strategies - and perhaps use a reverse KL to allow the RL to pick the most promising mode
DQN type agents (we used a margin loss in behavior cloning instead of a cross entropy loss)
Train RL agents without self-play and without a KL (leads to overfitting)
Hierarchical reinforcement learning to combine several of our reinforcement learning agents. It turned out that our single best RL agent was better than any combination of our top RL agents.
Combine the RL agents with rule based strategies - it turns out that it was hard to improve on what our RL agents came up with.
Overwriting the logits to -infinity for actions that are stated to have no effect (except for the idle action). For example: the right action when the player is already going right. The hope was that this would reduce the search space.
Mirroring the observation (and correctly translate the actions) to make sure that the player always has a y-value > 0, and that way cut the data space in half. We think that this did not work because either the game or the agents we clone are not symmetric about the x-axis.
Final remarks
We are happy to
share the submissions of our best WeKick and SaltyFish based agents
.
solutions.5th place:
TamakEri (“球蹴”) means “play with ball” in Japanese.
Congratulations to the winners! 🎉
Thanks to all participants, Kaggle team, Manchester City and Google Research for exciting games! ⚽️
Our team participated in this competition with about three weeks left to the deadline. We have been working towards winning by using reinforcement learning (RL). Fortunately, we got 5th place and we are happy to share our solution and
code
with the kaggle community.
Special thanks to my teammate
@yuricat
!!
Overview
We mainly trained our agents with (deep) reinforcement learning on a learner-actor architecture like
IMPALA
. Our neural network model is trained through self-play combined with single-play games against various opponent agents (rule-based bots, built-in AI, etc).
In the early steps of learning, we simultaneously used supervised learning (SL) with the top players' replays for the purpose of helping with the start of RL. The effect of supervised learning decayed as the training progressed, and the model was finally being trained only with reinforcement learning.
Our model consists of multi-head self attention, CNN, GRU, and MLP networks. The detailed model and input features are described later.
Our agents were mainly evaluated against a hard-level built-in AI (i.e. team difficulty = 1.0) that is implemented in the football game engine. On the last day of the competition, the win-rate of the latest model reached ~90% against the built-in AI and was still getting higher!
(However we found out just before the deadline that we couldn't submit the next model while scoring the previous model, so we couldn’t submit the latest (ensemble) model 😭😭😭 . We will make use of this experience at the next BIG match!! ⚽️)
Our implementation script
is based on OSS RL library
HandyRL
.
Algorithm and Training
Main algorithm
Off-policy distributed reinforcement learning
TD(λ) + importance sampling (clipped variant)
We used an off-policy distributed reinforcement learning to efficiently update an agent’s policy from the results of a large number of games. The learning algorithm is based on a policy gradient algorithm. The model learns policy, value, and return. Our value estimates final game outcome, and our return estimates discounted score reward. Then our policy maximizes both of them. In other words, the policy learns to maximize the expectations of scoring a next goal and winning a game. In our training, when one of the teams scores, the calculation of return is reset to break the episode down into before and after scores.
Losses
RL loss
Policy loss
importance sampling (1-step Retrace) * advantage * log(policy)
advantage = (value advantage + return advantage) / 2
value advantage = UPGO(λ)
return advantage = TD(λ)
Value loss
MSE
target = λ-value (TD(λ))
Return loss
Huber loss (SmoothL1Loss)
target = λ-return (TD(λ))
Entropy loss
SL loss
Policy loss
NLL (Negative Log-Likelihood) loss
target = replays’ action
Value loss
MSE
target = outcome
The advantage, which is used in the RL policy loss, is an average of value and return advantages. The value advantage is calculated based on UPGO(λ), which is combined with upgoing policy update (UPGO) and λ-value. The return advantage is calculated based on λ-return. The policy loss is calibrated by using a clipped importance sampling weight between behavior policy and target policy (1-step Retrace). The value target is computed based on a score difference with tanh to consider the degree of win/lose. That means when the score is 4-1, the outcomes of both players are tanh(4-1)=0.995 and tanh(1-4)=-0.995. When the score is 2-1, the outcomes are 0.76 and -0.76. In the beginning of the competition, we trained the model only with the outcome, so the above idea was used to encourage the agent to go for more scores. After that, we introduced the score as an immediate reward at the end of the competition. Now, we expect that the naive outcome -1(lose), 0(tie), 1(win) with immediate score rewards will also work fine.
The score reward (+1/-1) is used to calculate the return target with a discount factor. Note that we also tried a checkpoint reward similar to the one described in
the original paper
.
The percentage of supervised data in an experience buffer started with 10%. We manually reduced the ratio of supervised learning through training by removing the supervised data from the buffer. When the accuracy of the predicted action in supervised learning saturated, the ratio was set to 0%. From that timing, the model was trained only with reinforcement learning.
Training settings (see
the code
for details)
learning rate with decay (default=3e-8 x batch size)
optimizer: Adam
batch size: 156 ~ 400
buffer size: 3000 (min) - 30000 (max)
action repetitions: 4 (if an agent choose the action “→” at time t, “→” is repeated next four time steps t, t+1, t+2, t+3)
SL loss coefficient: 0.01
Computational resources
small experiment
worker: 96-core CPU
learner/trainer: 24-core CPU + 1 GPU (NVIDIA T4)
large experiment
worker: 96-core CPU x8
learner/trainer: 96-core CPU + 4 GPU (NVIDIA T4)
We used the small setting per experiment in the early phase. In the last three days, we leveraged large amounts of resources in parallel to accelerate multiple experiments (total ~4000 CPUs and ~20 GPUs). The final agent has played a total of ~700k games through the training.
Features and Model
Our model consists of several input features and modules.
Attention between players (encoder, multi-head self attention, control module)
The encoder module embeds the index of all players and game modes, and then encodes the embedding and some features to a fixed tensor
The tensor is fed to the multi-head self attention modules to get features considering attentions between all players
The control module mainly extracts (decodes) the feature of the active player using like an encoder-decoder attention mechanism based on the output from the previous modules
We also tried RNN as control module to manage a long horizon memory, but it didn't improve the performance so much
Action history (GRU)
The latest action history (sequence length = 8) is input to GRU for acquiring the context of actions
GRU outputs the latent features of the sequence
Left vs right player tensor (CNN)
This CNN is expected to learn the relationships between left vs right-side players with 1x1 conv and pooling (not for spatial structure)
This approach is based on
1st solution
of the NFL Big Data Bowl competition
Head modules (fully-connected networks)
Concatenates the features of the previous stages and feeds them into the policy, value, and return networks
Agents
Our neural network was trained through self-play combined with single-play games against various opponent agents. To keep the winning percentage at 50%, the weights of opponent agents were dynamically changed depending on the progress. The ratio of strong opponents increases when the training agent becomes stronger.
Self-play agent
The latest model is always used for self-play
The training is started with 10% self-play and finally ended up with 80%
Opponent agents when not self-play
Simple agents
Idle (do nothing), random, run right
Rule-based agents (Great kernel agents. Thanks to the authors!)
https://www.kaggle.com/yegorbiryukov/gfootball-with-memory-patterns
https://www.kaggle.com/eugenkeil/simple-baseline-bot
https://www.kaggle.com/mlconsult/1149-ish-bot-rl-approximation
https://www.kaggle.com/mlconsult/best-open-rules-bot-score-1020-7
https://www.kaggle.com/shotaro/optimizing-tunable-bot-with-optuna
Built-in AI
Hard-level AI (right_team_difficulty = 1)
Past trained agents
Agents created by multiple experiments
Mixed agents
e.g., built-in AI + RL agent, built-in AI + rule-based agent
Ensemble agent
By the end of the competition, multiple agents had been created. To further improve the accuracy of the policy, we tried an ensemble agent. The ensemble methods may include, for example, (weighted) voting of each agent and (weighted) policy averaging. We adopted the weighted policy averaging for the ensemble agent.

The win-rate of the ensemble agent achieved a highest score against the built-in AI in the local environment.
Evaluation
vs. various agents (1000-step game)
Some workers were assigned for evaluation to get the win rate during training. Some of the opponent agents are rule-based agents and the others are trained agents. The above figure shows the win-rate curves of a certain model at the time of saving the model. This graph shows our model was still getting stronger even at the deadline.
vs. built-in AI (full 3000-step game)
The win rate against built-in AI was used as a main metric to evaluate the performance of the agent. We evaluated 1,000-2,000 games to improve the reliability of the win-rate for the submission agents. We found that the rating of leaderboard is highly correlated to the win-rate against the built-in AI. The higher the win-rate against the built-in AI is, the higher the rating of the submission agent is. The win-rate of our final model reached ~90% against the built-in AI.
Additional features
New action set
In football, the direction of passing and shooting is important. We analyzed some matches and found that the kick and pass actions might be related to the sticky direction. So, we created a new action set that combined the two actions (Pass/Shot + Direction). With this extension, the quality of pass and shot was enhanced qualitatively, for example  crossing from side space, shot direction, free kicks, and so on.
New action set is like the following.
20 = LongPass + Left
21 = LongPass + TopLeft
...
28 = HighPass + Left
...
36 = ShortPass + Left
...
44 = Shot + Left
…
51 = Shot + BottomLeft
content_copy
Skipping initial steps
In a certain percentage of games during training, the initial frames were skipped by using the rule-base agents (e.g. 30% skipped games and 70% full games). This is expected to increase the variety of the states for the exploration and robustness of the agent. The number of the skipping steps was determined randomly at the start of a match After skipping, the training started from the state on the way.
Model distillation
We came up with a lot of ideas, but we didn't have much time left to create a new model from scratch. RL from scratch would take too much time! Therefore, we used a technique of model distillation (a.k.a knowledge distillation) to transfer the skills from the past model to the new one. At the start-up of training, the output of a pre-trained model was used as a teacher with reinforcement learning. As a result, the agent was able to beat the rule-based and other agents in a few hours. Note that it’s only applied in the early stages of training.
Deterministic opponent in self-play
We also used a deterministic policy for the opponents in self-play without frame skip (action repetition). As a result, the trained agent could always play against opponents who are stronger than itself, and it could be balanced with weaker rule-base agents and past models to achieve 50% winning rate.
Code
https://github.com/YuriCat/TamakEriFever
The implementation code is based on
HandyRL
, which is an open-source library for distributed reinforcement learning. The library can be applied to many problems of reinforcement learning. Because of its good parallelism, neural network training and episode data generation can scale easily. The simple implementation makes it easy to incorporate your game environments and algorithms into the library. We recommend this RL library for future simulation competitions, if you like it ❤️

Solution
Our solution itself is not too innovative and is simple. This competition can be approached in a variety of ways: rule-based, machine learning, and reinforcement learning. When I decided to tackle this competition in earnest, there were two teams Wekick and SaltyFish that dominated the other teams. Our starting point was the question of how strong an agent could we make if we could mimic the strong agents of these teams. We reduced it to a multi-class classification machine learning problem of predicting the actions of these strong agents.

However, we were able to achieve relatively high accuracy with the WeKick:18127517 or WeKick:18239675, so we focused on these agent's episodes. We tried combining them, excluding losing games.
Features
We generated 1154 features from the observations.
Some of them are directly from raw observations, but we used the following paper (in Japanese) as a reference to generate features based on the football domain.
https://www.i-juse.co.jp/statistics/xdata/sportscompe06-sem_special_award.pdf

The features we created are mainly as follows:
Distance and direction from the active player or ball to each player (polar coordinates)
Distance and direction of each player from the main location (center position (0,0), goal line (1,0),(-1,0)) (polar coordinates)
Distance and direction of each player to the center of gravity as a team (polar coordinates)
Maximum y-coordinate, minimum y-coordinate and their widths for the team excluding the goalkeeper
Maximum x-coordinate, maximum y-coordinate and width of the team
The x-coordinate of the offside line, and whether or not an offside position has occurred
The angle between the two goal posts and the ball

We also generated features for players/ball velocity and acceleration, but since the accuracy did not improve that much, we excluded them in the process to simplify the implementation.
Heuristics
Because of the bias in the frequency of occurrence of actions, we weighted the data according to the logarithm of the frequency of occurrence.
Also, many of the actions were the same as they were one step before, but we thought that the actions that were different from one step before (e.g., shooting, passing) were more important, so we gave them more weight.
Implementation ingenuity
We created the features without pandas because creating features with pandas seemed to be trapped by the 0.5 second per step limit, and there were times when we could not train with kaggle notebook due to lack of memory.
Since the agent has a 100MB capacity limit, the learning rate of LightGBM cannot be very small, so we mainly used 0.1.
Since the accuracy was in constant proportion to the score, I focused on improving the accuracy without having it play against other bots.

solutions.16th place:
Thanks to Kaggle, Manchester City F.C., and Google Research for this fantastic competition. Working on this competition was the most fun I've had for a while.
The tl;dr version of my solution is that I used an MLP model to stochastically imitate WeKick's agents, with some rules to help it navigate in unfamiliar waters.
After I got the GCP coupon, I looked at the competition timeline and thought that there is no way I can train a competitive RL agent from scratch in less than two weeks. I had to find some way to cut the training time shorter.
Then I found Ken Miller's
RL approximation notebook
and learned that the imitation strategy works reasonably well. So I decided to use a similar approach to (pre)train NN models to bootstrap my policy network, with an episode scraper based on Felipe Bivort Haiek's
Google Football Episode Scraper quick fix
. Huge thanks to both of you!
@mlconsult
@felipebihaiek
After a while, I found a lot of low-hanging fruits by tuning the features and assisting rules. As the model training is restricted to experience replays, no exploration was possible. The trained agent will not know how to act in a vast part of the state space, so setting some rules to guide them back to familiar territories can be quite helpful. I decided that tuning the imitator agents would be a better use of my time than an RL moonshot. Taking the safer bet paid off and gave me two agents with ~1,300 scores on the final day.
Some details (after some quick browsing, there seem to be a few teams using similar approaches to mine. I haven't read through them yet, so I apologize if I did not reference already-shared contents properly) :
Episodes: Only episodes in which both agents were high-ranking were used. It was most likely a mistake. It probably made my agents perform poorly when playing against low-ranking agents. A better approach might be a submission-based filter.
Features: Active-player-centered coordinates; coordinates and velocities of the goalkeepers are kept separately from the rest; distance-sorted coordinates, distances, angles, and velocities for the rest; Sprint and dribble sticky states; ball features; an offside feature(doesn't seem to work as expected).
Stochastic actions: I reduced the temperature of the softmax function (by doubling the logits). This seems to work better than deterministic/greedy actions.
Rules:
Using direction sticky states in features leads to overfitting and erratic behaviors, so I removed them. The downside is having the player high-passing the ball back to the goalie in free-kicks and resulting in own-goals. So I instructed the player to simply go right in free-kicks.
The model controls only the normal and throw-ins game modes.  Training the model to play other modes seem to be a waste of time.
No dribbling.
Sprinting is entirely rule-based. I had found this to work slightly better in the final days as it doesn't waste precious time giving the sprint command in critical moments.
Turn the player back when they are taking the ball straight out of the field.
The defense is the most tricky part. In early experiments, the models would give absurd commands when the ball controlled by other players is too far from the active player (possibly due to the lack of exploration during training). Therefore, I kept the agents on a tight leash when defending. The models were only allowed to take over when the ball is near enough or in high-passes; the running-towards-the-ball strategy is used otherwise. This approach gives away many easy shot opportunities to the other teams. Only on the last day had I realized that the leash was too tight for the latest models. Loosen the leash gave better results in local tests. Unfortunately, I only had two submissions left at that point, so I could not properly tune this hyper-parameter.
Local testing: At first, I let my agent play against the easy built-in AI and see if they can consistently beat the AI for more than five goals.  Later I've found that the larger goal margin in easy mode doesn't translate to better performance against high-ranking agents, so I switch to the hard built-in AI.
My code is public on Github(
ceshine/google-football-2020
). Currently, it lacks proper documentation and environment reproducibility. I'll try to make it better in the coming days.

solutions.25th place:
Solution Summary
First I applied imitation learning (i.e. behavioral cloning) to train a good model, and then used it to initialize the weights of my reinforcement learning agent.
PPO was then used to train the agent again a fixed set of opponents from public kernels. a KL divergence term was added to stabilize training.
Last of all, I adopted self-play to allow the agent to self improve and used "league training" to avoid self-play from breaking down.
My final solution is RL agent + minor patch on defense using fixed rules.
Detailed account of my solution can be found in this blogpost:
https://flyyufelix.github.io/2020/12/02/google-football-rl.html
Source code
I used stable-baseline3 written in Pytorch for RL training. I made several minor changes to incorporate pre-trained models, better model saving, and added the KL term.
Other tools I used including hydra for managing hyperparameters, Weights & Biases for visualizing the rewards and logging, and docker for standardizing the dev environment.
My source code for imitation learning and reinforcement learning training can be found here:
https://github.com/flyyufelix/google_research_football_kaggle

introduction:
== Description ===
The National Football League (NFL) has teamed up with Amazon Web Services (AWS) to develop the “Digital Athlete,” a virtual representation of a composite NFL player that the NFL can use to model game scenarios to try to better predict and prevent player injury. The NFL is actively addressing the need for a computer vision system to detect on-field helmet impacts as part of the “Digital Athlete” platform, and the league is calling on Kagglers to help.
In this competition, you’ll develop a computer vision model that automatically detects helmet impacts that occur on the field. Kick off with a dataset of more than one thousand definitive head impacts from thousands of game images, labeled video from the sidelines and end zones, and player tracking data. This information is sourced from the NFL’s Next Gen Stats (NGS) system, which documents the position, speed, acceleration, and orientation for every player on the field during NFL games.
This competition is part of the NFL’s annual 1st and Future competition, which is designed to spur innovation in athlete safety and performance. For the first time this year, 1st and Future will be broadcast in primetime during Super Bowl LV week on NFL Network, and winning Kagglers may have the opportunity to present their computer vision systems as part of this exciting event.
If successful, you could support the NFL’s research programs in a big way: improving athletes' safety. Backed by this research, the NFL may implement rule changes and helmet design improvements to try to better protect the athletes who play the game millions watch each week.
The National Football League is America's most popular sports league. Founded in 1920, the NFL developed the model for the successful modern sports league and is committed to advancing progress in the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of sports-related injuries. Health and safety efforts include support for independent medical research and engineering advancements as well as a commitment to work to better protect players and make the game safer, including enhancements to medical protocols and improvements to how our game is taught and played. For more information about the NFL's health and safety efforts, please visit NFL.com/PlayerHealthandSafety.

Code Requirements

== Evaluation ===
In this task, you will segment helmet collisions in videos of football plays using bounding boxes. This competition is evaluated using a micro F1 score at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.35.
There are a few important differences from other bounding box metrics:
The main departure from a traditional metric is that some imprecision on the timing of the impact is acceptable.
For a given ground truth impact, a prediction within +/- 4 frames (9 frames total) within the same play can be accepted as valid without necessarily degrading the score. Assuming the player is moving over the course of those frames, the exact bounding box predicted to achieve an IoU of 1.0 would also vary depending on the frame.
As one helmet may partially obscure another from the camera's perspective, both predicted and ground truth bounding boxes may overlap. However, at most one prediction will ever be assigned to a given ground truth box.
The two criteria described above mean that one or more predictions could theoretically be assigned to more than one ground truth boxes. If this happens, our metric will optimize for the assignments between your prediction(s) and the ground truth boxes that lead to the highest total number of True Positives (thereby maximizing the F1 score). At most one prediction will be assigned to any ground truth box and vice versa.

solutions.1st place:
Thanks to the organisers of this competition, it was a very interesting task to solve!
My approach was very similar to the other top solutions: 2d detection of all helmets, tracking of helmets, 3d classification of crops and post processing to suppress false positives.
Detection
I used the YoloV5-l trained on 10k images using the full resolution.
I started using EfficientDet based detector with modified set of anchors to better match the helmet size distribution and trained on video frames, but YoloV5 worked better.
Helmets Tracking
For each detected helmet, I found the optical flow between a few surrounding frames.
I tried to use either OpenCV or RAFT (Thanks
@daigohirooka
for the great notebook and referring RAFT). I used the optical flow to track helmets between frames and to estimate the average helmet velocity on the image plane over a few surrounding frames. I think RAFT worked slightly better but my top submit still used OpenCV for helmets tracking.
2.5D Classification
For classification I used 16x3x128x128 crops, scaled so the median helmet size over the current frame is mapped to the center 40 pixels. It provides the consistent scale, robust to detected bounding box variations, especially for partially visible helmets.
I also corrected for the linear helmet movement between frames. The current frame at 8th slice is always centered, but all the other frames are shifted using the current box velocity, estimated during the tracking stage. So when the player is running with the constant speed or camera is panning, the helmet stays at the frame center, but during acceleration it would move to and from center.
The intuition behind - the acceleration is important for classification, but it's harder to estimate on top of potentially fast movement due to camera movement.
For classification models, instead of 3d convolution I used the
Temporal Shift Module
:
TSM has very little overhead comparing to N 2d models, can reuse any ImageNet pretrained 2d classification model and performed reasonably well for video understanding tasks.
I also had promising results with the
MotionSqueeze: Neural Motion Feature Learning for Video Understanding
approach, which adds flow estimation to TSM based model, but the implementation is not trivial and does not have license specified.
I found small models with TSM added at the start of residual blocks work well and are usually easy and fast to train (from an hour to a few hours per model). I used the ensemble of EfficientNet B0-B3, Resnet18 and Resnet34. When comparing the TSM approach to 3d convolution, it's easy to notice the lack of pooling in the time dimension, so instead of shifting features by one frame, I shifted by 2 and 3 frames in the last blocks of resnets/efficient nets to mimic the dilated convolution.
During training I marked 3 frames around the impact as positive and used 5 or 10% positive samples.
In addition to annotated training labels, I added the false positive prediction from a few undertrained detection models. I used 4 folds CV, for submission I averaged predictions of multiple models from all 4
folds. To speed up prediction, I ran classification on a few fast models first, to filter 95% of simple to predict negative samples.
Post-Processing
The postprocessing is quite simple, I select the detected/classified box with highest impact confidence and use flow/tracking information to suppress the detections for the same player for surrounding frames, with suppression decaying from the current confidence to 0 over 16 frames. I used the same threshold for all video files and frames.
I checked if such post-processing would suppress the positive samples using training dataset and found surprisingly significant amount of positive samples within 3-10 frames for the same player. Most of such sequential impacts were of the different type, for example helmet to helmet impact followed by helmet to body. To address this, I changed the classification model to predict the impact type as well, and suppressed the predicted impact type only. The score improvement was quite small, less than 0.01 estimated on local CV.

Here's the solution from the team
