I found that 10 repeats of 10-folds seemed to be a good choice to assess the validation scores.
For my baseline method, I used SVC, which had a validation score of 0.367 +- 0.025 std.
I used the features provided by Tanoi and found that including 'kidney-failure' resulted in a cross-validation score of 0.370 +- 0.025.
I also grouped features based on their names and added up their values. For example, I added up the values of features that contained the words pain, loss, or inflammation. Including the summed-up features containing the word pain improved the cross-validation score to 0.375 +- 0.026.
I also included polynomial features and selected a feature pair that resulted in the highest cross-validation score: 'back_pain' and 'yellow_skin', this gave a score of 0.3937. Next, I further tested including additional pairs of polynomial features ('itchiness', 'bullseye_rash', and 'diarrhea', 'hypoglycemia'): the corresponding validation score further improved to 0.3989.
Feature selection: I preselected some algorithms that performed well on the initial feature set and checked what would be a good VarianceThreshold cutoff rate for them. I tested XGBClassifier, SVC, BernoulliNB, NuSVC, and LGBMClassifier. All of them resulted in the highest cross-validation score when using a threshold of 0.1. These were all the algorithms that I used for the final ensemble without weighing.
The public score of my final submission was 0.37089, and the private score was 0.52302.
Here's what did not work or might have worked:
Due to the vast amount of original features in the dataset, I thought that clustering techniques would be beneficial to this task. title: Lux AI Season 2: Terraform Mars!
introduction:
== Description ===
Introduction
As the sun set on the world an array of lights dotted the once dark horizon. With the help of a
brigade of toads
, Lux had made it past the terrors in the night to see the dawn of a new age. Seeking new challenges, plans were made to send a forward force with one mission: terraform Mars!
Welcome to the Lux AI Challenge Season 2!
The Lux AI Challenge is a competition where competitors design agents to tackle a multi-variable optimization, resource gathering, and allocation problem in a 1v1 scenario against other competitors. In addition to optimization, successful agents must be capable of analyzing their opponents and developing appropriate policies to get the upper hand.
All code can be found at our
Github
, make sure to give it a star while you are there!
Make sure to join our community
discord
to chat, strategize, and learn with other competitors! We will be posting announcements on the Kaggle Forums and on the discord.

== Evaluation ===
Each day your team is able to submit up to 5 agents (bots) to the competition. Each submission will play Episodes (games) against other bots on the ladder that have a similar skill rating. Over time skill ratings will go up with wins or down with losses and evened out with ties.
Every bot submitted will continue to play episodes until the end of the competition, with newer bots playing a much more frequent number of episodes. On the leaderboard only your best scoring bot will be shown, but you can track the progress of all of your submissions on your Submissions page.
Each Submission has an estimated Skill Rating which is modeled by a Gaussian N(μ,σ2) where μ is the estimated skill and σ represents the uncertainty of that estimate which will decrease over time.
When you upload a Submission, we first play a Validation Episode where that Submission plays against copies of itself to make sure it works properly. If the Episode fails, the Submission is marked as Error and you can download the agent logs to help figure out why. Otherwise, we initialize the Submission with μ0=600 and it joins the pool of All Submissions for ongoing evaluation.
We repeatedly run Episodes from the pool of All Submissions, and try to pick Submissions with similar ratings for fair matches. Newly submitted agents will be given an increased rate in the number of episodes run to give you faster feedback.
Ranking System
After an Episode finishes, we'll update the Rating estimate for all Submissions in that Episode. If one Submission won, we'll increase its μ and decrease its opponent's μ -- if the result was a draw, then we'll move the two μ values closer towards their mean. The updates will have magnitude relative to the deviation from the expected result based on the previous μ values, and also relative to each Submission's uncertainty σ. We also reduce the σ terms relative to the amount of information gained by the result. The score by which your bot wins or loses an Episode does not affect the skill rating updates.
Final Evaluation
At the submission deadline on May 8, 2023, additional submissions will be locked. From May 8, 2023 to May 4th, we will continue to run games. At the conclusion of this period, the leaderboard is final.

solutions.1st place:
First of all, I have to acknowledge
@ttigga
and
@danmctree
for co-producing the most uncertain and stressful race to the finish I could have imagined. Huge congrats to both of you.
Background
The Lux game specification can be found
here
.
Overall Strategy
I competed in the
Lux Beta
just before this competition began, but threw out most of my strategic code when the post-beta rule changes were announced. The major change was that lichen now produced power. I decided then that I'd really push lichen growth early and often to generate as much power as possible. That mostly stayed true throughout the competition, even when robot-produced solar power was being promoted as a viable alternative. I just didn't have the discipline necessary to keep a robot stationary for long - there are so many other things for it to be doing!
My state-of-the-art visualizer
Forward simulation
I would determine actions for all units and factories, update state, then do it all over again. I'd do that for about 2.9 seconds every invocation, which gave me anywhere from 5 to 50+ steps worth of planning, depending on unit count and pathfinding complexity. I simulated just about everything including my future units. I tried to guess at opponent unit movement in limited combat situations. I never added logic for handling self-collisions or my factory explosions - probably due to optimism that maybe it'll work out differently when we get there! I assumed opponent lichen values were static, which was never correct, but never too far off.
Factory placement
Basically: adjacent to ice, close to ore, close to no-/low-rubble territory. I went back and forth on the relative value of nearby ore vs nearby flatland. Flatland can be incredibly valuable during the early game. Instead of digging (expensive), my light robots can go antagonize nearby opponent lights (cheap), throwing off their early plans. But I can't just avoid ore and end up completely outnumbered by mid-game. I eventually added some logic for measuring ore scarcity and comparing my current factories' ore situations vs my opponent's to determine a dynamic bonus for ore proximity. There's also the matter of ice vulnerability/security (i.e. can this location readily be denied access to ice), but I'll cover that in more detail shortly.
Mining resources and building robots
My strategy largely depended on growing lichen until my power income was greater than my current (estimated) power usage. Then I'd build some units and go back to mining ice and growing lichen - until my power income was ready for more units. This was definitely not a perfect strategy but it worked ok. I tended to err on the side of under-building units so that I always had plenty of power to hand out. I never knew for sure how to decide when to build a light vs save metal to build a heavy. I tried to maintain some minimum number of lights per factory and then build heavies beyond that point.
On chains
I used chains heavily during the beta, to limited success. My code was error-prone, and it seemed too easy to disturb a whole chain of activity with only a single light robot. I decided early on I would avoid chains except in the trivial factory-adjacent case. Clearly Tigga and Siesta proved me wrong in the end. Their economic system based on chains is definitely superior. I was rarely able to adequately disturb a chain for long. And using chains allows for more flexible factory spawn locations - ice no longer necessarily needs to be factory-adjacent. All resources are just 1 chain away! Very powerful.
Roles and Goals
For every step I simulated, I would set or update a "role" and "goal" for each unit. A role is a long-term but non-permanent job/responsibility. A goal is a single multi-step objective that typically involves movement and/or hitting some resource or power threshold. Each role controlled a different goal state machine. The current role and goal would be persisted between invocations. Every step I would:
Check each unit to see that the current role is still valid
Check each unit for special role transition situations
Iterate over all units, assigning roles to units without one, until all units had a role
Update goals for all units
I ended up with about 10 unique roles: antagonizer, attacker, blockade, cow, miner, pillager, protector, recharge, relocate, power_transporter, water_transporter.

Prioritizing Action Selection
Not all units are created equal. I didn't want a low-priority light robot to claim a cell that a heavy robot urgently needed to move to, or pick up power that could be better used elsewhere. I used a list of prioritized situations to ensure a reasonable order that units (and factories) locked their actions into place. I wrote some nifty python to do this in a relatively clean way.

Ice Conflicts
During sprint 2, I noticed some matchups would incidentally result in two factories fighting over ice. It felt like a crazy idea at the time, but I figured it might be worth purposely choosing an otherwise suboptimal factory spawn position if it meant I was well-positioned to deny ice to an opponent’s factory, while using light water transporters to outlast them. I called this strategy “ice conflicts”. I started doing this during sprint 2 by giving a huge boost to my final factory placement if it was within 4 distance or so of all nearby ice deposits around an opponent factory. This led to my agent winning sprint 2, and temporarily breaking Kaggle’s matchmaking algorithm, sending my score to 36k+ (RIP Homeostat). I figured this strategy would be copied or countered but it never really was. While Bovard was fixing the matchmaking algorithm, I deactivated the ice conflict logic from my “production” build to save it for a rainy day (i.e. the last day). I continued to make improvements to this strategy, including using a pair of light "blockade" units to block opponent water transporters. In the end, ice conflict spawning is the only thing that kept me competitive with Siesta's and Tigga’s improved economic strategy. Interestingly, this did not work at all against flg, who tended to use heavies to flexibly move ice around the map wherever it was needed. This resulted in very few factory kills, and I just had to live with the otherwise suboptimal factory placements. This weak matchup really hurt my final score.
Coordination Among Units and Factories
There were a few situations where units and factories needed to coordinate with one another to make sure they weren't trying to do/use the same thing.
Enforce unique unit->cell assignments
Units would claim a cell whenever they were tasked with digging/antagonizing/standing there.
Some units could “displace” another unit’s assignment, invalidating its role and forcing a new role to be determined. This usually happened when a heavy took over a job from a light.
Enforce unique unit->unit assignments
Only really relevant for units with the attacker role. I didn't need more than one unit pursuing an opponent unit at a time.
Enforce unique cell->factory assignments
Ice cells are assigned to my various factories over time, determined by whichever factory sends a heavy robot there first.
This ensures factories can rely on relatively stable ice income over time (no risk of “losing” an ice cell to a friendly factory)
Any unit can mine any ice cell if its available, but if a unit belonging to the owner factory wants it, they get it, displacing whoever was there previously.
Collision avoidance
As described earlier, units determine their actions in priority order. This means I often needed to determine if a high priority unit could safely move to a cell currently occupied by a lower priority unit. Eventually I settled on simply comparing the low-priority unit's power to the power necessary to move
anywhere
, assuming at least one safe move was possible. Similarly, I needed to check for situations where a high-priority unit might move onto a cell that was the only remaining safe option for a lower-priority unit to move
to
. These checks were a little messy, and there were still small gaps in the logic, but it worked most of the time.
Reflection / Looking Ahead
I had very few expectations coming into this competition. I had no idea how much time I was going to put into it, and I was mostly under the impression that RL was going to reign supreme as in season 1. The game proved to be very challenging, surprisingly deep, and well balanced. I so enjoyed tinkering on this project for 3+ months. Thanks to
@stonet2000
and
@bovard
for putting this all together. And a special shout out to the folks who were constantly pushing the bounds of the game/meta:
@harmbuisman
,
@danmctree
, and
@ttigga
. And to
@ferdinandlimburg
and
@philippkostuch
who pushed radically different and competitive solutions over the last month or so. I look forward to seeing you all on future leaderboards.

solutions.2nd place:
With the competition still ongoing I've no idea whether I'm going to end up 1st or 5th (though judging by the first few days I suspect it'll be 1st-3rd, which I'm very happy with!), but now is the time for the writeup while it's still fresh in my mind!
General outline
I went for a stateful rules based bot with no full forward projection, though with some internal forward projection. I wrote it in Typescript. Early on I was planning on doing a team entry with some other Screeps players, but that fell through.
Most of my work was done with self-play, especially for the first couple of months where I had some tricks that other people hadn't figured out yet which I wanted to keep under wraps. Pretty much all of them other people figured out on their own though! This got a bit tricky as per-step runtimes of my agent climbed, with some self-play games taking >20 minutes. I think next time if we're still at 1000 steps of 3 seconds, I may drop down to C++ as I got to the stage where I'd needed 10+ hours on an 8 core machine to get any sort of reasonable data. Season 1 at 360 steps of 3 seconds was much more managable.
Placement and bidding
In general I felt everyone was bidding too low throughout the season, but I didn't want to bid higher, because then others would bid higher. Only my final agents bid "high" at 41, chosen because other agents were using 40 as their limit. Bidding was based on a simulation of best placements, then running things through my scoring system. I do rarely bid -1, as placing second was very rarely judged to be an advantage. I set the max range for a resource to be 4 from any factory tile. I noticed others had this set further. I found I'd too often have my chain stalled out if this was the case, but maybe I should have based it on range to enemy factory after everything had spawned. While the majority of my mining was chains I did have support for non-chain stuff which occasionally kicks in.
Placement was designed to focus on good spots with both ice and ore. Having ice within one tiles was heavily prioritized, and having it outside of two was heavily penalized. Rubble and map edges were also penalized. Aggression, where my factory was closer to a resource than the opponent's only source of that resource, was a big bonus, again with ice more important than metal.
If good ore+ice spots could not be found I tried to place ice-only factories, or, to pair with ice-only factories, ore-only factories. I then had metal and water couriers to move resources between them.  I'm not sure I saw anyone else doing metal couriers: I reasoned it was better than spawning myself and moving the robot as often ice only factories would have an excess of power. Not 100% sure this was true.
Robot logic
I went for a stateful rules based bot. Each robot was spawned to fulfill a "role", and each step each robot would generate the actions to fulfill that role to its best ability. Some roles were quite static, like mining along a chain, while others were given more freedom. In cases where decisions were based on the "target" of another robot, I'd take the latest information - either from something previously run this tick or something run last tick. Everything was iterated through in the same order to keep things stable. The commands could get complicated enough to fill my action queues fairly well (go here, dig that rubble, go back to factory, pickup power, go here dig that other rubble was plenty!)
Once those actions were generated they were passed through a check to see if those actions would change the queue, and if not, nothing was submitted.
All robots went through the same core "starting" logic where they'd do urgent tasks irrespective of role which went down a common path:
Clearing lichen urgently (ie. where there was an opportunity to cut lichen off)
Clearing rubble urgently (to reconnect my lichen),
Giving power urgently (usually to a heavy that was at risk of being killed)
Fighting neighbours
Safety logic was also shared - I had a very important and expensive
checkSafetyForAction
function which would try to figure out if any enemy robot could kill my robot before I made it back to the factory. This was a bit more complicated than simply knowing how much power I needed to return home (which I also had) and I didn't really ever get perfect. If a robot "unsafe" or going to become "unsafe" it would ignore it's previously computed set of actions and either go home for more power or sit still and charge.
At the end of every step I'd have a resolver stage that figured out collisions, repathing and bumping/swapping, as well as validating pickup/transfer commands to avoid waste, and adding new transfer commands if they were better than what the robot wasn't doing. I then had a final "emergency" bump logic for when everything else failed and a robot needed to move. Everything else shouldn't have been failing… but there were corner cases in cramped environments that sometimes fell through the cracks.
Robots could transition between roles. For example rubble clearers who got dragged away from their desired target by too much would turn into combat robots. Less important robots could be moved to a different role if a more important role was stuck waiting for metal. Things like that. I feel this was an underdeveloped part of my bot. Often I'd over-provision a role and not have anything stealing the robot for another role. For example: I might over-build rubble clearers, transition them to combat, then realise I needed more rubble clearers after all and not transition back.
Factory logic
Lichen growth was one of the trickiest parts to balance as it was rarely clear what the best strategy was. Others have proposed "only do it at the end" and maybe that's correct, though most of the top agents disagree. I tried to balance efficiency (eg. not watering when at 100, trying to minimizes the losses in the ceil(numTiles/10) function) with need for power and the current water situation. I had a forward projection for late game which helped a lot earlier in the event, though once late game attacks on lichen started appearing it became a bit too conservative and often I found myself holding on to too much water at the end.
Weaknesses/"future work"
While I don't plan on doing any future work, if I did, there are things I'd take a step back on re-write.
Movement in crowded situations. It often ended up a bit too much "first come first serve" with lots of cancelled queues due to blockages. I feel I could have analysed this better to form better queues.
Countering late game heavy lichen blitzing. Seems I lose a lot of games to this. Have to figure out a way to indentify it and combat the blitzers. I tried this with my 10pm final day submission, but it was too rushed. Many games I lose despite being 4x lichen up at step 900 and basically dropping to zero by step 1000.
Less movement. My robots tend to be a bit twitchy and waste power. More "doing nothing" would benefit it.
Better handling of "mobbed" factories (and mobbing myself). A factory can quite easily be denied ice if it's surrounded by enemy factories. Right now I don't really do that.
In general, better attack/defend priorities. It's not really focussed enough right now. For example, I've seen it stop camping the ice of a factory with very low water where camping it would have killed the factory.
Maybe more solar-panel stuff?
solutions.3rd place:
While the final games of Lux AI 2 are playing and I'm still uncertain of my final ranking in what's still looking like a close 2-5th place, I thought I'd do a little (long) writeup. I thought this was an exciting competition to take part in, with a deep and very well balanced game that really rewarded different types of strategies. I think we probably only just tapped the surface level of this game, and I'd definitely recommend checking it out even post-competition for fun or perhaps research
Approach
My main approach in this competition was to use C++ logic forming as a skeleton for a large selection (about 1500) of custom parameters that I would tune using custom made statistical analysis tooling. Everything from target selection to combat micro and move conflict management was deeply affected by these parameters. These parameters ranged from serving as a desire adjustment for further tiles, factory spawn tile evaluation, to booleans that could adjust critical if statements or even turn entire functionalities off to overarching multipliers like META_SIMCITY, which would adjust my strategic level desire for peaceful actions (collecting resources, clearing rubble) versus aggressive actions like trying to kill enemy units or digging up enemy lichen. I tried to get most 'opinionated' logic captured in at least some parameter so that I could discover whether my intuition was good. It often was, but there were some real stinkers in there too
I chose this approach because I know it's a very reliable way for me to do well and because it's a lot of fun. I think it combines some of the good parts of rule based bots, such as the ability to really calculate out an optimal solution in places (eg. pathing) and a certain flexibility in strategy and game mechanics, while also taking some of the good parts of reinforcement learning, such as your software slowly intuiting optimal proportions of types of actions. I do believe that reinforcement learning strategies may have somewhat higher potential here, but I didn't go for that as the process has always felt a little unpredictable to me, and just not as fun. And well, I'm not a research group with the available hardware funds to achieve it reliably
Parameter Optimization
I tried to tune my parameters by running a lot of games, in each of which I'd randomize a significant proportion of the parameters (normal distribution for floats, uniform for ints). On every game I'd generate a file with the values of all parameters, whether I'd win or lose and also an assortment of game statistics I thought might be useful, for example the amount of light units I built, the amount of turns units spend digging rubble, the starting rubble on the map, etc. Then, outside of the game in my stats tool I built for halite 2, I would check to see if there was any way to improve the parameters.
For that, I've tried several approaches and rewards. For rewards, some options I picked were chance of victory, the lichen difference with my opponent, the amount of power I produced, the match making rating of associated versions, and even a neural net output trying to estimate my matchmaking rating based on statistics such as the proportion of time my units spend mining ice.
Using this reward, I'd try to find better values using several automatic and manual methods: I've used basic statistical tools such as the Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient to see if there was a slope in the data (perhaps I'd win slightly more often if I made my units dig a little bit more ore). Neural nets and random forest tree learning approaches to try to find better values. Just plain old average values of integers or weighted averages of floats. And sometimes I'd just stare at graphs myself and hope to make sense of it. Basically I treated the parameter reward space as an unknown noisy multidimensional function to find a maximum on, but generally made the assumption that complicated interactions between the parameters would be small enough that I could fairly effectively hillclimb by adjusting individual parameters on their individual contributions. I just couldn't generate data fast enough to try and work with anything else
I picked this type of approach over more standardized approaches like simulated annealing, because the amount of games I could run was tiny compared to the amount of parameters I had and there was a lot of noise and I was constantly changing the code as I went. Under those circumstances, that approach doesn't tend to do well
After parameter changes, I'd check to see if there was an improvement on the leaderboard, and revert if not. The leaderboard was extremely noisy, so that may not always have been correct, but I figured it'd be correct more often than not. A nice advantage of this stats orientated approach is that I could often make improvements with low time and brain commitment. I would often take 5 minutes to automatically tweak and upload a new version or two before work, and then the same before going to sleep. Some of my biggest periods of growth were in weeks I had no time to mess with the code while doing this learning
Initially I mostly had both of the agents in a game randomized and learning, for a double learning rate. Later I switched to static reference players to better track my progress. In the end I'm still not quite sure which is better. Static reference players give purer data, but less of it, and I felt there's some advantage in playing against more randomized players too to prevent overfitting.
Some lessons learned here were:
This learning approach, even despite all of its randomness, is pretty good at finding the low hanging fruit of improvements
It's also very inconsistent and has a lot of trouble finetuning less important parameters in all the noise.
You would think that if you have thousands of clean datapoints, where you know for sure a causation exists, and you take some parameter and your odds of victory get a Pearson correlation coefficient of 1.05 and a corresponding p-value of 0.0000001 for the null-hypothesis. And on top of that the average victory odds of that parameter are in fact observably higher on a graph. That if you then adjust this parameter upwards, you will start winning more, at least locally. Nothing could be further from the truth, almost every time it will have absolutely no measurable impact. I don't know what this implies, maybe just that I'm bad at stats, but I feel like there has to be some kind of fundamental effect here that consistently overexaggerates or invents apparent effects where there are none. I know it's not just that sometimes with many parameters you just hit the low p value odds, because it consistently happened to more parameters than you would expect. I feel like I might take some time post competition to more properly explore this
Victory chance was probably overall the most effective at getting results. Optimizing for mmr or opponent win rate did almost nothing for me this time (but was very effective in halite).
I found that varying my used reward seemed to work a bit better than consistently applying the same one. Likewise with the used approach for tweaking values. Some rewards I think had insidious side effects, such as if you optimize for proportion of turns spend digging, combat units may want to start dying on purpose. By varying rewards, that effect is limited a little
Manual adjustments using a combination of the Pearson correlation coefficient and my insight into the games generally gave me the most gains. Automatic tweaking using Pearson was fairly effective too. For that I generally used:     newvalue = oldvalue + (abs(oldvalue) * pearson * scaler), sometimes with a max change, or requiring a p value below some level. At the start I was very careful, using a low scaler ( < 1), later I discovered using a fake parameter simulation thing, that high scalers and frequent tweaks actually get you to the best value much faster, even with lots of noise and low sample sizes ( < 1000). That did seem to work better, though I often had to manually correct drift. I had a few parameters doing absolutely nothing, and these drifted from  1->0.88,  2->3.81, 3->3.7, 4->2.75, -5 -> -5.39. Which honestly wasn't that bad. Meanwhile actual parameters I must've initially estimated wrong could shift by a factor of 10-100 over the course of the competition, I presume for the better
Using neural networks and random forest trees to try to predict improvements was a waste of time. I think there just wasn't enough data, and enough random noise in parameters for extreme overfitting.
Correlation between local results and the leaderboard were not great but tolerable
It was critical to have a parameter indicating my version number, and to adjust the reward based on the average for that version. This erased a lot of weird artifacts and allowed me to fairly reliably use data across different versions without too much of an impact on results
In the end I probably would've honestly done a little better if I didn't spend so much time on the parameter finetuning, and instead spend more time designing deep game specific algorithms and by watching games and fixing bugs, but I think the experience I gained using this approach was probably more valuable
Graphs and power
As a fun side effect of collecting in game data, I could easily find interesting observations and draw cool plots. Honestly I mostly underused this, but there was one graph that had a huge impact on my strategy. But first, let's introduce lichen power generation for those less familiar with it.
For every lichen tile you had, you would generate 1 power per turn. Power was a super critical bottleneck, so that's pretty nice. To create lichen you need to spend water at your factory to water your tiles. This costs ceil(tiles/10) water for both new and already existing lichen tiles. On turns you don't water, all your lichen tiles decay by 1. In most games, most water comes from ice mined by heavy units. You can expect to spend a minimum of 12 power per water, plus probably a bit of loss on inefficiencies. Now much has been analyzed about this mechanic already, but the basics are that ignoring weird integer cutoffs of the watering, you can expect that on a turn that you're watering, you have a cost of 1.2 power per tile, and a gain of 1, for a total change of -0.2. On tiles that you're not watering, you have a gain of 1 power per tile. So if you alternate watering and not watering, you can expect a gain of 0.4 power per tile per turn while keeping your lichen field intact.
This sounds pretty good. By just spending a bit of upfront power, you can grow a large, profitable lichenfield, which additionally is your source of points at the end of the game. Through the power gains, you could invest back even more into the factory, collecting more ice, more lichen, more power. About 1-2 months into the competition, I think the dominating thought was that this was a totally obvious way of making economies work.
The main catch was, that it didn't actually really work. Now, results may be a bit different for other players, but for me it looked like this:
This is a graph with on the x-axis, the amount of ice I've collected throughout the game ). On the y-axis, it's my total ice profit. Both are divided over starting factory count. Ice profit here is the amount of power I gained from my lichen, minus the amount of power I spend digging for lichen-ice (ice used for the factory upkeep is not counted). The blue lines are different fit lines,  purple dots are victories, red dots are losses. The green/red line shows the running average with red meaning few data points
Now I see two main things here. First, I never really made all that much of a profit from ice, on any game. Second, the amount of ice I collected doesn't affect profits as much as you'd hope. The only reason you seem to get a bit more profit on the far right end, is that those are overwhelming victories. For the bulk of games and for losses, there might even be a bit of a downward trend. Now critically, this graph did not include the rubble clearing costs and move/requeue costs necessary for the process. If I include the rubble clearing costs, you get this graph:
On top of this seeming lack of profits, most of the gains tend to be at the very end of the game where power isn't as useful anymore. Basically, big lichen power is a scam! There's no profit here. Reasons why range from the awkward shapes lichen fields often have to form, which means you require longer water investment stages, to enemy units clearing out your rubble.
Of course you need the points so you might as well water the lichen early to at least sort of run even. But it just isn't quite what it was chalked up to be. Anyway, all of that is just kind of to illustrate that collecting data of this kind can be super useful. In this case, it lead me to go for unit based power generation much earlier, and made me realize that the popular lichen canals used were actually not that good of an idea. While they saved you rubble digging costs of digging out everything around the factory, the shape of the lichen actually meant you ran a bigger loss on the lichen itself, and additionally canals were very vulnerable to harassment.
On the other hand, building units for power generation was much more obviously profitable. You just need to have your units stand still often enough that they don't just burn their generated power. This was far from trivial in a many units style approach like mine. Clogged situations around factories in particular can force many moves when scary enemy units pass by and you gotta handle your conflicts so that units don't run into each other. Getting units to calm down and stop clogging was always one of my largest battles. In the end, most of my units ended up self sufficient, never taking any power from the factories so that I could just direct most factory power to making more units. Here's two graphs showing ice and ore based power profits in a typical game for me (ice profits here ignore rubble costs):
Replay viewer
Besides my stats tool, I also used a custom replay viewer designed for my own replay format, which was arguably even more useful. I generated the replay data from within the code of my agent, allowing me to visually present not just objective game data, but also various forms of debugging data.
Here's a quick peak of my replay viewer. The shape of units shows their movement. The fill of units shows their power for easy at a glance viewing. There's some little side-things too like highlights for unit deaths (magenta) and transfers (yellow) and a water carrier highlight.
This image shows the 'base' desires for every tile on the map, this corresponds to how much units will want to go there, before unit-specific adjustments such as distance from the tile
This viewer was insanely useful for debugging purposes. It's much easier to see what is going on when you can easily see it across the screen like this instead of having to dig through logs. For example, I had an bug in my spawning logic at some point, where I messed up an x and y coordinate, so factories would be preferably spawned on the same column as tiles adjacent to ice. Probably would never have found it if I didn't spot the weird vertical lines in my spawn desire output
For anyone who likes frequenting these kinds of competitions, I'd strongly recommend taking the time to invest a bit in both a reusable custom replay viewer and possibly your own tool to analyze stats. The time invested in any such infrastructure easily pays itself back through ease of debugging, and it's otherwise a great learning experience.
Speaking of learning experiences. I largely chose c++ as my agents language of choice because I wanted to learn the language. That task mostly failed, in that I ended up mostly just sticking to some really basic usages of the language, but at least it was much more performant than alternatives might've been. I mostly used an ugly but effective style, where I had a large collection of global variables I could easily access everywhere at very low performance cost. One critical trick is to precompute everything you can precompute. Perhaps my most used thing throughout the codebase is to iterate over the neighbors of a tile. It was a huge help to just precompute that all once at the start, and never have to worry about performance impact and literal edge cases anymore. Outside of one awkward O(n^2) algorithms that went haywire near ~900 units I never really experienced timeouts. The game still was rather sluggish locally, but a significant part of that was I/O I couldn't really speed up without a total redesign. Oh yeah, preprocessor definitions to avoid logging overhead is cool
Long, accurate action queues were very beneficial here, I mostly did queues through going turn by turn into the future, having every unit determine its course of action for that turn, resolving any move, transfer or pickup conflicts and then forward simulating the next turn. It unfortunately failed quite frequently, especially when units had to adjust for combat, made others scoot over, which then prevented transfers from landing, etc. Overall though my requeue costs were not that bad because I at least got the heavy units on the mines adjacent to the factories (and solar panels) to work predictably. The one thing I really wish I could've done is some system to really have significant information from predicted further turns carry back down to earlier turn in the queue. That unfortunately proved a little too challenging for me to come up with a good performant system, maybe in a follow-up competition!
Throughout most of the competition and until the very end I've been in a tight race with a few other competitors. In particular ry_andy_, Tigga and Harm Buisman. Later to be joined by reinforcement learning player flg. Thanks to them for making this competition very exciting and of course to Stone Tao and to Bovard Doerschuk-Tiberi for organizing this and creating such a fun game. Hope any of that helps someone and I guess I'll see some of you in some future competitions!

1. Introduction
Lux Season 2
LuxS2 is a two player, zero-sum game in which each participant controls a swarm of robots racing to terraform Mars faster than their opponent. It is played on a 48x48 square map in multiple phases:
A simultaneous-move bidding phase to decide who goes first,
A sequential placement phase in which players place 2-5 factories (number chosen randomly) and
A simultaneous-move main phase.
During main phase players acquire metal to create robots, water to grow lichen and clear rubble to make space for the lichen farms. At then end of 1000 turns the player with the larger lichen amount wins.
The main phase is split into 20 day-night-cycles, each lasting 50 turns out of which 30 are day and 20 night.
There are three types of actors:
Factories grow lichen, produce robots and turn raw ore/ice into usable metal/water,
Heavy units excel at combat and resource gathering but are somewhat sluggish to move around especially in high-rubble areas,
Light units are good at moving around efficiently but mine less resources and lose in combat to heavies.
Units require power for almost all actions. Power is gained each turn by factories, slowly by all units during the day and by growing lichen. A unit without power cannot take any actions and needs to (slowly) recharge.
When two units collide (move to the same target position), heavies destroy lights and among same units of the same type the one with more power wins. This collision handling also applies to your own units!
On top of these mechanics there is also a planning component: players can send a queue of up to 20 actions to each of their units. This is useful since each time the action queue is updated, a small power charge needs to be paid by the affected unit. Example:
A heavy unit digs 20 times (60 power each) and the dig action is sent each turn anew (10 power per update): power cost: 20 * 60 + 20 * 10 = 1400.
Same case but a queue of 20 dig actions is sent once: 20 * 60 + 10 = 1210.
The unit used almost 15% less power in the second case. Power is pretty much the scarcest resource so this efficiency gain makes a very big difference.
Comparison with last season
The game increased in complexity compared to last year quite a bit:
the map is 2.2x as large,
a match lasts 3x as many turns,
there are three different game phases,
for learning approaches, like mine, the power system (especially in combination with the need to clear rubble to gather resources and grow lichen) made random exploration a lot harder,
the action queue system changed the game from a single-step problem to a multistep  planning one.
2. Method
Plan
The matches of the competition are run on Kaggle using CPU-only VMs that seemed to have varying performance but mostly be single-core machines. Because of this performance was the main consideration on every decision and I came up with a plan focused on it:
Simplify the action and observation space to manageable size,
Handle collisions and action queues,
Use imitation learning and small map RL to find a neural network architecture that combines CPU-performance, large receptive field and sample efficiency,
Train a small model using RL,
Train a larger main model using the small one as a teacher,
Optimize the final model for cpu inference.
Action and observation space
Action space
I structured my model to have seven different actors:
Bid: Discrete(10): [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 70, 100, 150, 200],
Spawn location: Discrete(48*48),
Spawn resource amount for water: Discrete(7): [50, 100, 120, 150, 200, 250, 300],
Spawn resource amount for metal: Discrete(7): [50, 100, 120, 150, 200, 250, 300],
Factories: Grid(4): [noop, build light, build heavy, grow lichen],
Light units: Grid(23): [moves in 5 directions (incl. noop), dig, self-destruct, pick-up all power available, transfers in 5 directions for [ore, ice, power]]
Heavy units: Grid(23): same as light units.
Grid(k) means a 48x48xk action space in which for each position of the 48x48 map one of k actions is sampled independently.
On transfer actions a unit transfers everything it holds for ice and ore and 90% of it’s current value for power. When performing a spawn action, a location and a starting resource amount for water and metal need to be selected at the same time. I first sample a location then predict the water/metal amounts for all locations in parallel and sample one of the 7 actions at the chosen spawn location.
Note: there are no actions for transferring or picking up refined resources like metal and water. So the agent could only use unrefined resources for transferring over long distances.
Observation space
I encoded  the positions of all actors using 0/1 variables, most other quantities (power, resources, rubble) were taken as continuous variables normalized to usually be in the -1 – 1 range. I tried using explicit embeddings for all discrete observations but couldn’t find any difference in performance. The one exception to this was the lichen ownership: each factory has its own lichen strain. With up to five factories per player that’s eleven discrete values when you add one more for “no lichen”. I embedded these using a 16 dimensional embedding layer and summed the result with a 16-dim embedding of the player id to indicate the owner of  that lichen.
Global features like the current turn or the spawn resources remaining are encoded as separate feature layers (with the same value repeated for every position in the 48x48 feature layer).
In total this gave me 54 different features. To these I added historic information: the positions and resources of all actors as well as lichen and rubble values on the board for the last three turns (17 features per turn). The final observation space had a shape of 48x48x105 (54 + 3*17=105).
Collisions and action queues
Collisions
Self collisions were very punishing this season since all but one of the colliding units died. During early RL I realized that my agent avoided having units work next to each other and in general didn’t like making many units. This seemed to be caused by the fact that a somewhat random policy (which is needed for exploration) will cause many harmful self collisions. To counteract this I canceled all moves that would result in self collisions, so that units performed a noop instead. This required reproducing quite a bit of game logic but it increased (early) learning speed a lot.
Action queues
To fill the action queues with multiple actions at inference time I used forward prediction: the agent predicts actions for itself and the opponent then steps the environment and repeats the process. Since the opponent’s action queue is part of the public game observation, I had one agent on the LB that used it for forward prediction (and falling back to its own prediction if no move from the queue is available) – it performed similar to just using predictions.
During training I did not use action queues and only had the agent predict its next action. This method only had one problem: the amount of power used to update action queues differs in both cases. This causes the agent’s expectations about how long it can mine, which parts of the map it can reach etc. to be off for longer sequences. To combat this I used an expected communications cost approach: I randomly applied the comm cost with p=0.2, simulating an average length five action queue (which was pretty close to the effective action queue length that the agent achieved after all optimizations).
Neural network architecture search
I used some beta agents and later a few early submissions to create a dataset for imitation learning (IL). More precisly, I:
downloaded around 2000 matches from top-scoring agents via MetaKaggle
transformed the obs and actions into the spaces mentioned above when creating the dataset
stored everything as compressed HDF5 dataset (the final dataset was around 300GB and HDF5 allows for very fast random access without loading everything into RAM).
Submissions that used actions I did not support were excluded (some agents were trasferring water between factories).
I evaluated different NN architectures based on their unit-accuracy on this dataset (I also trained and evaluated for factory- and spawn-locaction-accuracy but these were much easier to learn). The main traits I was looking for were:
CPU performance
Receptive field (“see the whole board quickly”)
GPU-Memory usage
Sample efficiency.
The best result I got was a “DoubleCone” network, a DoubleCone(4, 6, 4) is depicted below. It performed a decent share of its compute  at a downscaled resolution of 12x12 (instead of 48x48) which helped with respect to all goals above except sample efficiency. To avoid a loss of fine grained control there is a skip connection around the DoubleCone-block. Additionally before and after that block there are multiple full resolution ResBlocks. The actor heads are simple 3x3 convolution layers without activations, the one exception to this is the bidding head, which uses the critic architecture (minus one Conv-Layer).
The critic is depicted above, its architecture did not seem to be very important in my tests. The slightly unusual AdaptiveAveragePool is there since many of my early RL tests were done with 16x16 and 24x24 maps and I wanted a truly resolution-independent architecture.
I also experimented with layer optimizations, especially ResBlock design. Here I tested recent advances from computer vision (e.g. ConvNext) with some task specific optimizations. Some results:
I did not use any Bottleneck or InverseBottleneck blocks as the 1x1 convolutions are fairly GPU-intensive but do not provide receptive field.
I used way less activations, in particular there is no activation at all after the second convolution, only SqueezeAndExcitation.
With my compute budget I couldn’t find real differences between ReLU, LeakyReLU or GELU.
3x3 and 5x5 convolutions performed similarly if you roughly double the depth when using 3x3s (lower parameters / receptive field).
There are no normalization layers as I couldn’t find any benefit in them, as long as there are SqueezeAndExcitation layers. Without these performance dropped significantly but part of this could be recovered e.g. with LayerNorm.
A comparison between my final architecture and a ResNet can be seen here:
Reinforcement Learning
My agent was trained using self-play and reinforcement learning. I used shaped rewards that were strongly focused on the game result to avoid biasing the agent as much as possible.
Rewards
In a set-up phase (around 65M steps) the agent was trained using heavily shaped rewards focusing on gathering resources. It received rewards for:
moving towards its closest resources
clearing rubble from resources
mining resources
moving to closest factory when carrying e.g. > 100 resources
dropping resources on factories
bonus for mining ore and ice
making units
growing lichen
placing factories near resources.
These rewards were “selfish” for each agent (not zero-sum).
After this phase, I switchted to zero-sum rewards:
{-1, 0, 1} for game result
[-1, 1] for relative lichen advantage at the end of the game
0.3 for each factory
[-0.8, 0.8] relative unit advantage
[-0.1, 0.1] for relative lichen power production.
Each reward was given relative to its opponent's performance to yield a zero-sum reward in the range of [-1, 1]. One exception was the factory reward: here the agent received a flat + or - 0.3 for each factory it had more / less than its opponent. Rewards were only given when a change was made (e.g. when the factory was lost), not each turn afterwards. This way the (undiscounted) sum of all relative rewards equals the relative advantage at the end of the game.
I tested many different reward weightings over the course of training and the agent seemed very robust to changes, probably because the game result and lichen advantage dominate the reward.
Reinforcement learning method
My RL method uses a single-learner-multiple-actor approach. I implement everything using Python’s Multiprocessing: each actor  and evaluator is its own process and all processes communicate via queues. The architecture can be seen below. I use Pytorch for all NNs and vectorized compute but no RL framework.
In the beginning I tested PPO and Vtrace for advantage calculation on 16x16 and 24x24 maps and achieved similar results. I went with Vtrace. All in all my agent learned using the following losses:

I lowered the entropy very slowly over training and updated the teacher regularly, keeping it around 30M steps behind the agent.
One problem with my approach was that bidding and spawning factories are fairly rare events, they only occur on ~1% of all steps. This meant that a typical batch of size ~500 contained 0-2 of these events which didn’t allow stable learning. To counteract this I “upsampled” spawns and bidding by having a dedicated spawn actor. Every 16 update steps this actor played around ten matches from the starting position for roughly 50 steps each then abandoned these games.
Training larger models
It was my plan to only use the DoubleCone(4, 6, 4) network shown above as a teacher for a second and maybe third generation of larger models. However due to problems described below with runtime performance, I had to cancel the training of a DoubleCone(6, 8, 6) model after around 100M steps. I then continued finetuning the smaller model. Its training performance can be seen here:
Optimizing Kaggle Performance
The fact that each unit had to pay an engergy cost when updating its action queue meant that solutions that only predicted few steps ahead had a strong disadvantage. Over the course of the competition I ran many local and leaderboard tests to evaluate the impact of energy efficiency. Results were fairly consistent: one should aim for at least 4-6 step predictions, below that performance was crippling (especially single step). Getting more steps only provided modest advantages in my tests. Some results can be seen here:
When you compare these results with prediction performance of ResNet and DoubleCone architectures, you can see that large models were very hard to use. See below. The 24 block ResNet is similar to what was used by last year’s winner and it would barely be able to predict a single step.
One very important detail is that no fast inference runtime (like onnxruntime with platform-specific execution providers like OpenVino mentioned above) was available in the Kaggle environment. Since it wasn’t possible to install any packages, me and a couple of other competitors tried packaging onnxruntime ourselves but as far as I know no one was successful. The fast execution providers like OpenVine somehow weren’t working on the competition environment (although it worked everywhere else including Kaggle notebooks). It also was close to impossible to debug this as all error logs were 404 for me.
When looking at the performance numbers above and the fact that for example OpenVino doubled/tripled performance in all my tests, it was clear it was make or break for using larger models on Kaggle hardware. After unsuccessfully debugging the issue for a couple of days, I decided to give up on it, cancel the DoubleCone(6, 8, 6) model I was training and went back to fine tuning the smaller one.
After this I tried many other approaches for speeding up inference:
static post-train quantization
dynamic post-train quantization
model compression
jit trace and script.
Most of these either failed as they had some kind of setup time which was too long on Kaggle hardware or they had unfavorable accuracy-performance trade-off compared to using a tiny model to fill up action queues:
Filling up action queues
My agent usually managed to predict 3-5 steps ahead using a DoubleCone(4, 6, 4). To improve on this, I used transfer learning with a DoubleCone(2, 6, 2) network with only 64 (instead of 128) channels. The action queues were then built as follows:
Predict up to 3 step with the DoubleCone(4, 6, 4) network.
Fill up with predictions from the tiny net until time runs out.
Use pattern matching to fill the queue to 20 actions.
Always doing 1-3 slow predictions meant that any mistakes made by the tiny net during previous predictions would be corrected. This way the agent usually managed 6-8 predictions, with effective (corrected) queue length between 5 and 6.
The pattern matching used common behaviors to naivly fill the queue: units moving constantly back and forth in combat, (light) units picking up power and transferring it to adjacent mining units and digging. If none of these worked, it just copied the last action.
For switching between these stages I used predictive time management. This was necessary as VM performance was somewhat unreliable.
Transfer learning was done with a (Q)Dagger-inspired approach: first training on the teacher’s trajectories and then switching to the student’s to correct remaining mistakes. The strength of the teacher was reduced over the course of training.
3. Conclusion
The competition was a bit of up and down for me. On the one hand the lack of fast deployment options for NNs was a huge letdown and the debugging problems made it very frustrating to work with. On the other hand the environment was very interesting and fun to work with. My solution worked quite well and I had a chance to use a wide array of tools from IL and architecture search over RL to transfer learning and performance optimization. But most importantly the community especially on Discord is just amazing. Lots of thanks to Stone Tao, Bovard and the sponsors for running this competition! Thanks to Agenlu for helping with performance optimization, Tigga, ry_andy_, Harm and SiestaGuru for being the people I battled with the most and finally thanks to ry_andy_ and loh-maa for (unknowingly) providing an IL dataset.

Deimos's RL approach
Background
Our colleagues participated in the Lux Season 1 competition last year and conducted an in-depth study on the competition environment. During the preparation phase of this year's competition, we were invited by Stone to rewrite the Lux environment using JAX framework, which resulted in considerable speedup effect (overall user experience still needs improvement and we plan to optimize further in the future). Therefore, we also wanted to participate in Lux Season two to gain first-hand experience.
Method
Our policy for this competition remains the utilization of the PPO algorithm, and the specific implementation follows the off-policy approach provided in RLlib. Since the observation space of this season's competition environment is structured similarly to that of the previous season, we have adopted the neural network architecture outlined in [1] for the backbone of our model and have made our code available as a reference in [2]. However, we have also made some modifications to our model that are unique to this season's competition environment, which we will highlight in the following sections.
Feature space
The feature space consisted of three main components: global information, map features, and action queue. Each component was designed to capture critical information that allowed our robot to operate efficiently in the given environment.
Global Information
The first component of our feature space is global information, which includes the current time phase of the environment (step, cycle, hour) and the total number of robots and resources. We utilized one-hot encoding to represent certain features, resulting in a feature dimension of 32.
Map Features
The map feature component contained information about the resources (lichen, ice, ore, rubble) present in each block as well as the robot (unit, factory) located in each block. The feature dimension was designed to be 48x48x30.
Action Queue
The last component of our feature space was the action queue, which represented the current set of actions in robots' queues. This component had a feature dimension of 48x48x20x6.
To encode our feature space, we then replicated this encoded global information for each grid. We used ResNet to merge the three components to achieve maximum efficiency.
Action related
The biggest challenge for RL players was managing the massive action space in the second season. To address this, we restrict the number of actions sent to a robot to one per turn, i.e., we completely ignore the action queue, and turn it into a real-time control problem. Unlike flg's approach, we allow the action to be repeated, thus some power can be saved. Besides, we implement a relatively complicated conditional sampling as follows.
Sampling Order for action sequences
We sample different dimensions of action in the following order.
Action type (move, transfer, pick up, dig, self-destruct, recharge, do nothing)
Action direction (5 directions)
Resource type for action (ice, ore, water, metal, power)
Quantity of resources for action (float, 0-1)
Infinite repeat or not (boolean)
n (integer)
The dimensions sampled before affect the dimensions sampled later, so the whole action spaced is modeled as a conditional probability distribution.

Continuous Value Sampling
From the action space of the unit type robot described above, we can observe that the quantity of resources operated is a ranged real value, such as $[0,1]$. Generally, for actions involving continuous numerical values, researchers usually model them as a Gaussian distribution, but the gaussian distribution is unbounded, so some truncation is needed. Here, we adopted a more reasonable distribution, the beta distribution, which falls into $[0,1]$ by nature. The advantages of this approach can be found in our reference at [3].
Model Architecture
In brief, is an 8-layer-deep 64-neuron-wide Resnet with some additional feature pre-processing layer and action/value head. The backbone is the same as [1], and the specific implementation can be found in [2].
Training && Performance
Random Initialization
The distributed reinforcement learning framework consists of two types of processes:
Rollout worker : interact with the environment to generate data, and
Trainer :  perform policy optimization.
As this competition is a perfect information game, we set Rollout worker to play against itself, i.e., self-play. However, we found that the model did not explore new game states during the training process. Therefore, we downloaded a large number of replays from the Kaggle, randomly selected various game state from them, and used these intermediate states as the initial settings for the self-play process. This helped our strategy to explore many game situations that were difficult to evolve through self-play, and the data download can be referenced via the Lux season one sharing blog.
CURRICULUM LEARNING PHASES
There are three main phases during the training process.
dense reward + rule-based factory spawning
dense reward + neural network factory spawning
sparse reward + neural network factory spawning
Phase1
The reward is set to dense reward as shown in the table below, and in this phase, we wrote a script for choosing factory spawning location and initial water/metal. In addition, if a player loses the game, it will be penalized by a large negative reward, which cancel out all its past reward. Thus, only the winner get positive reward in this phase.

Phase2
The dense reward as described above is still used in this phase, but the factory spawning is now decided by the neural network. This phase is quite short. As long as robots know how to collect resources during phase 1, neural networks can learn to spawn factories in a few hours.

Conclusion
Our training gets a smooth start, and we can see the ELO score increase steadily. However, it was stuck around 1900 in the last two month. We did lots of experiments to improve the ELO score, but none of them worked. In general, our approach is quite similar to flg's. Both ours and flg's follows last year's champion's approach, but in detail, we have different action space modeling, different rewards, and different curriculum learning phases. Maybe there is a bug; maybe our action space modeling is too complicated; maybe our reward is not good enough. We can't figure out the reason, because RL system is too complex to debug. It consists of too many components, and each component has too many hyper-parameters. Most time, if you did wrong in one component, you just get a bad ELO score silently without any explicit exceptions. Despite all the above, we still want to share our approach with you.

This was my first time competing in a competition of this kind and building a logic bot. I have found it extremely interesting to compete and recommend it to people who were on the fence about joining this year. It is a great experience to code your bot and then visually see it perform against other bots. The game design has been superb, creating some new types of challenges. There have been a few pitfalls for me in this competition, which I would like to share with you. Hopefully, this will help some people avoid them in the future.
In this post, I will first quickly explain the game. Then I will go through my design. After that, I will go through my pitfalls and end by going through what I would have liked to do if I had had more time.
Python Code
For anybody interested in the code, it's stored on
GitHub
.
Game Summary
The LuxAI 2 challenge is a 2-player zero-sum game where both players compete to terraform Mars by building the most lichen in 1000 time steps. They start with a few factories and enough resources to build a few units. During the game, the units can collect two types of resources—ore for building new units, ice for keeping the factories alive and watering lichen. Lichen, besides counting for the score at the end of the game, also generates power that units need to perform actions. In general, power was a very scarce resource in this game, so efficient power usage was essential.
There are two types of units: a light unit which is more power-efficient, and a heavy unit able to dig more per turn and therefore has higher resource utilization. Units execute actions and require power to perform these actions.
If two units collide, the stronger one survives. If they are the same type and one unit is stationary, that one is lost. If they are both moving, the unit with the most power survives. When your units collide with each other, the same rules apply. Therefore avoiding collisions between your units is extremely important. This wasn't easy because you control your unit not by sending its next action but by updating an action queue which can easily consist of 50 actions. One could update the action queue for every unit at every step, but this is quite costly, as it costs power every time you update the queue.
Final design
I switched my design around a few times during the competition, but in the end, I ended up with the following design.
Factories decide on strategic focus
Each unit is assigned to the factory that spawns them, and the factory will decide, based on its current resources, the game time step, and the goals that it already scheduled, what currently is the highest priority strategy for its units to focus on. Some examples of these strategies are to increase lichen, collect ore, attack the opponent or defend a lichen tile. Based on these strategies, an attempt is made to schedule the most suitable unit for this task. The unit selection picks the unit that, at a glance, appears to have the highest value per step (explained in more detail in the get_best_case_value_per_step section). If none of the factory's units can be scheduled to aid in this strategy, an attempt will be made to schedule a unit on the next highest priority strategy. After a factory schedules a unit, the factory recalculates the priorities of the strategies again to decide where to schedule the next unit. This loop continues until all units are scheduled, or no unit can be scheduled on any relevant strategy.
Units carry out strategic focus with goals
I ended up with 11 different goals for units. These goals either directly contribute to fulfilling a strategy or help the unit survive( e.g. fleeing from opponents). For example, these goals include collecting ice at a specific coordinate (x, y), clearing out rubble at a specific coordinate or destroying a specific opponent's lichen tile. The abstract base class of these goals have the following methods: get_best_case_value_per_step, generate_action_plan and get_value_per_step_of_action_plan.
get_best_case_value_per_step
To evaluate goals, I used the following simple formula:
value_per_step = (power_benefit – power_cost) / nr_steps
This method, at a glance, estimates this formula for the best-case scenario of scheduling a unit on a goal without computing an exact action plan. To estimate the power benefit of each goal, I created a formulate which contained some parameters I could tweak. Then to decide on the parameters, I tuned them based on the performance on the leaderboard.
To quickly compute the best-case scenario, we assume that everything is optimal. E.g. to collect ice for a unit, we would calculate the distance it would take to go there without being obstructed by any unit, there to be no rubble on the way, and the unit max number of digging the ice out is based on the state to be day meaning that power is generated each step and then goes back to the factory to return the power.
These best-case values for goals are used to select the most suitable unit for a strategy. E.g. if we want to increase ore to build units, all units belonging to a factory that are not scheduled on a goal yet, are asked to compute their best-case values of mining ore on the ore tiles around them. The unit with the best value is selected, and for this unit, we will carry out the expensive method, generate_action_plan.
generate_action_plan
To get from a goal to an action plan, a specific set of actions, you will need some type of planning algorithm. I used
A*
as the basis. A* is an algorithm similar to the more famous Dijkstra's algorithm but can better prioritize the most promising node if you can set accurate lower bounds on the remaining cost to reach the endpoint. In a grid world, as in this game, a reasonable lower bound can be obtained based on the distance to the final node. Goals are broken down into some subgoals (e.g. move to a factory and pick up power, collect ice and transfer ice to the factory) to reduce the planning horizon, which improves computational performance significantly. However, the found solution can be slightly worse than the optimal solution.
Another crucial task to solve is ensuring that your units don't collide. This is especially hard in this game, as we are not planning one step at a time per unit, but we update action queues containing multiple actions. For our planning algorithm, this means we must also consider other units' action plans. In the end, I used a reservation table for this. Which works in a first come, first serve manner. The first unit to be scheduled will reserve the time coordinates (x, y and t=time) corresponding to its action plan. Then any future unit planning will not be allowed to be on those coordinates and will generate its action plans accordingly.
get_value_per_step_of_action_plan
Given that we now have the exact action plan of the unit, we can calculate the value per step of this plan precisely. It was essential to do this, as in the middle game, often there are more units than worthwhile goals to carry out. If you always schedule your units on goals, you end up using too much power, and then your units will eventually have too little power left for the most important goals. Therefore, goals with negative values are never scheduled.
Pitfalls
All units performing the same strategy
At the start, every unit thought for themselves what the most worthwhile goal was, and they were not assigned to a factory. Using a
sum-assignment problem solver
, units were assigned to specific goals. This has one big drawback. Often all units ended up performing the same goal. E.g. if the parameters of ice mining were slightly more favourable than ore mining and there were many ice resources around the factory, the units would only collect ice, neglecting the ore resources completely. Then I would end up with a lot of ice but no ore to build new units. Similarly, if ore mining was slightly more favourable, I might end up with many units but no ice and, therefore, no lichen to generate power for these units.
Therefore, some self-balancing rules were required in the planning algorithm. I ended up scheduling units to perform goals based on their factories' needs. After the factory schedules a unit on a goal, it recomputes its most important strategies using the last scheduled unit's goal. For example, suppose the factory scheduled the last unit to collect ore. In that case, it will soon build new units, so it will now prioritize the strategy of generating power for these future units.
Optimal goal resolution
The biggest pitfall I spent a lot of time on at the start was attempting to compute the perfect joint plan at every step. I was using conflict-based planning for this. The idea of this algorithm is that first, every unit comes up independently with its action plan to complete its goal. After this, we validate whether the joint plan is valid, i.e. does it not contain any collisions? If any units' paths collide, we split the problem into two sub-problems, one where the first unit is granted the time coordinate and one where he isn't. Then, in my implementation, I would reconsider the best distribution of goals given this restriction (if a unit is not granted its optimal path, it might be better to have the unit perform a similar goal on an unblocked path). Then the unit that was not granted its optimal path will generate a new action plan. If this is invalid again, we split the problem in two another time. In a branch-and-bound style, we focus on sub-problems whose optimal value is most promising and repeat this process until a node is found with the best-case joint value and without collisions.
At the start, this worked out well and created joint action plans which were always optimal. But as I started to build more efficient economies and my unit size increased, collisions increased, and no collision-free joint plans were found in time. To solve this, I spent significant time optimizing the code to generate action plans under the time limit. But it appeared impossible to get this to work. Therefore, in the end, I switched to using a reservation table, which, although might not grant the perfect solution, is magnitudes faster and allowed me to focus computational resources and, more importantly, my available programming time for this project on more important parts.
Under-utilizing logging
I underestimated the complexity of building a bot to control 100+ units. At the start, when a bug popped up, I figured out the problem using the debugger and carried on. But there were two big disadvantages in mainly using the debugger vs logging. One was that matches often took more than 20 minutes, so replicating this state in debug mode was time-consuming. Also, there were some recurring problems which are harder to detect in debug mode. For example, I had some situations where some units were scheduled on a goal, but then another unit got scheduled on the same goal. The original unit would be unscheduled but would later schedule themselves on this goal. Detecting this takes a decent amount of effort using a debugger, especially when other units are scheduled in between as well. But this is very easy to detect by logging every scheduling and unscheduling decision.
More parameter optimization and better evaluation
The best way to know if your bot is improving is by comparing it against opponents on the leaderboard. Therefore it is essential to make good use of your five daily submissions. Unfortunately, I focused too much on adding in all the functionality needed for the bot, planning to focus on optimizing the parameters at the end. But in the end, I realized there was a lot more I wanted to test than the number of uploads I had left. Looking back, I should have started using all my uploads from the start, as it takes little effort to tune a few parameters each day.
To make the best use of these uploads, it helps to evaluate them as accurately as possible. Kaggle's rating system jumps around a lot, especially before the final submission date. For leaderboard reasons, this might be optimal, but for accurate performance evaluation in a day of games, there might be better options. I haven't found much information on the Kaggle rating system, but I believe it works similarly to the
Elo
and
Glicko
rating systems. In these systems, the impact of recent games is more important than that of old games. This makes a lot of sense for the original domains of these methods, sports. But for static bots, you can be more accurate by using a method that assumes a stationary level of the competitor.
Improvements if I had the time
Changing the goal-scheduling method
During the competition, I set up my scheduling in two different ways, both with their shortcomings. When units schedule purely by themselves, they might end up performing goals irrelevant to the factory. On the other hand, when factories focus only on the most critical strategy, this might lead to poorly accomplishing the most important strategy instead of efficiently accomplishing the second most important strategy. I would have wanted to combine the two methods by multiplying the goal's value by the strategy's importance. The importance of the strategy should then be a number whose average value is approximately 1.
More focus on attack/defence goals
Initially, I spent most of my time getting the planning algorithms to work correctly, quickly enough and without collisions. Later, I struggled with balancing my economy. There was also a lot of small functionality to build in, e.g. differentiating between a unit's private action plan and the action queue it sends to the environment and precisely calculating the power of this action plan, including the moments it will update the action queue.
In the end, I ran out of time to properly implement the defence goals and also some attacking goals. I did implement clearing out the opponent's lichen decently, but defending ice tiles close to my base or defending my lichen was rushed and did not work properly, nor was it prioritized appropriately by the factories. Neither did I have the time to implement camping important opponent resources or capturing opponent's units low on energy and far away from their factory, where they are safe. Lacking these capabilities hampered the performance of my bot severely.
Conclusion
In conclusion, it has been a great experience. I want to thank Stone Tao for creating such a rich competition environment. I have learned a lot by competing here. I hope this write-up helps some people avoid my pitfalls for the next challenge. And lastly, I can't wait to see what LuxAI Challenge 3 will bring!
