solutions.34th place:
One of my favorite things to do is write up the solution afterwards, so I'm glad I got a rank good enough that I feel comfortable regaling you with all of our exploits.
This was a very interesting problem, especially hot after finishing
the Mercari competition
which was also big on text analysis. Prior to this competition and Mercari competition, I had never done textual analysis before.
I originally got excited by this competition and worked on it a bit early, but got turned off when the test set leakage was announced, so I left to focus on the Mercari competition. I was very excited when this competition got extended, because it let me work on this in the final month and apply everything I learned from Mercari. Pretty much all this work was done in the last month of the competition.
Our final model was a weighted average of submodels, one of those
blend of blends
everyone talks about. Let's dive deeper into that.
The Final Level 3 Weighted Average
Final toxic model = 0.713 * Model A + 0.011 * Model B + 0.142 * Model C + 0.134 * Model D
Final severe toxic model = 0.231 * Model A + 0.443 * Model B + 0.279 * Model C + 0.047 * Model D
Final obscene model = 0.146 * Model A + 0.2 * Model B + 0.309 * Model C + 0.345 * Model D
Final insult model = 0.371 * Model A + 0.005 * Model B + 0.250 * Model C + 0.374 * Model D
Final threat model = 0.204 * Model A + 0.524 * Model B + 0.124 * Model C + 0.148 * Model D
Final identity hate model = 0.318 * Model A + 0.412 * Model B + 0.141 * Model C + 0.129 * Model D
For each of the models, the predictions were transformed to ranks prior to being averaged together. This ended up being important for the five-fold CV (boost of ~0.0002), but didn't seem to impact the Public or Private LB scores.
The five-fold CV (5CV) was 0.99231, 0.9874 on the public leaderboard, and 0.9872 on the private leaderboard. 5CV for toxic was 0.98877, for severe toxic 0.99242, for obscene 0.99566, for insult 0.99039, for threat 0.99460, and for identity hate 0.99203. Notably, while the 5CV score was 0.0003 higher than any of the submodels, the public and private leaderboard score was identical to Model B, at least down to the four digits that Kaggle reported.
It was cool to see that each one of the four models was the highest weighted model in at least one of the six labels.
The weights for the model were found by adapting
Tilli's automatic weighted blending from the Mercari competition
. I had talked a lot in this forum about finding weights by hand (trial and error) and had done so with my final weights until the very last day, when I gave the automatic approach a try. Doing so made the model ~0.00003 better, and in a competition where every inch counts, I guess I'm happy I did that.
The Level 2 Stacker Models
I was very bullish on doing some Level 2 stacking with tree-based models. While it backfired for me
in the
Porto Seguro competition
(my first competition), I thought it would do well here because of the multi-label interactions -- I thought that a model trained for toxic could, for example, help inform not just the toxic prediction but also the predictions for insult, obscene, etc. So thus I made four Level 2 models.
My level 2 models (Models A, B, C, and D) were all trained on the same 757 features -- 334 of those features are 5CV out-of-fold predictions of Level 1 submodels and the other 423 features was handcrafted feature engineering.
Model A was a LightGBM with 20% column sample.
Toxic, threat, insult, and identity hate were trained with 15 leaves and a learning rate of 0.02, whereas severe toxic and obscene were trained with 4 leaves and a learning rate of 0.005. I found this parameter mix via Bayesian hyperparameter tuning. I used early stopping to find the right round limit for each label, but then hardcoded that round limit across all the folds, rather than use early stopping on a per-fold basis, as I found per-fold early stopping to produce some overfitting. Model A had a 5CV of 0.99208, a public leaderboard score of 0.9873 and a private leaderboard score of 0.9871.
Model B was an XGBoost with 10% column sample
, a scale_pos_weight of 5, and 0.01 gamma. Again toxic, threat, insult, and identity hate were best going deep -- I trained each with a learning rate of 0.005 and a max depth of 8! Severe toxic and obscene were best with a max depth of 3 and a learning rate of 0.01. Surprisingly, the correlation between the predictions of the XGB and LGB was just ~0.92, so it looked like they might average well to produce a boost. This boost happened on the 5CV score. Model B had a 5CV of 0.99203 (total level 3blend was 0.99231), but the  public leaderboard score of 0.9874 and private leaderboard score of 0.9872 matched the results from the total level 3 blend.
Model C was a neural net with bagging
, implemented in Keras, that took the input through a RELU dense layer with 64 units before outputting into the final 6 unit dense layer. Tuning revealed that using dropout, more units, or a more complex architecture resulted in a lower score. The batch size was 32 and it was trained for three epochs. Because it trained so fast (20 seconds per fold), I decided to use bagging and ran the NN 20 times with a random 80% of the rows sampled with replacement for each bagged run. Model C had a 5CV of 0.99140, a public leaderboard score of 0.9868 and a private leaderboard score of 0.9862. While clearly worse than Models A, B, and D, it added well to the average, at least in terms of 5CV score. The use of bagging produced an increase of 0.0001 on the 5CV score of the NN.
Model D was a random forest with 500 trees
using entropy split, balanced class weight, and a 'min_samples_split' of 10 and 'min_samples_leaf' of 5. Toxic, threat, and identity hate had a max_features of 0.1, insult had a max_features of 0.2, and severe_toxic and obscene had a max_features of 0.3. Obscene and threat used max_leaf_nodes of 100, toxic, severe_toxic, and identity_hate had max_leaf_nodes of 200, and insult had max_leaf_nodes of 500. Model D had a 5CV of 0.99120. I trained it last minute on the penultimate day, so I never submitted it to the leaderboard.
Each of these Level 2 models were trained five-fold with the predictions for the fold combined together via rank transformation. This was important for making the fold average 5CV match the overall 5CV, but did not impact the Public or Private LB scores.
The Feature Engineering
A lot of Kagglers bemoan feature engineering, but I think it's the one thing I'm really good at and is what makes up for me being bad at neural nets. (If you're good at neural nets, but bad at LightGBM tuning and feature engineering, I think we'd make a great team in a future competition!) I liked feature engineering here because I think these features pick up a lot that TFIDF and neural nets miss. For here, I dumped the entire kitchen sink at the problem and produced 423 unique features:
Basic feature engineering:
number of words, number of unique words, unique words per word, number of characters, number of capital letters, number of lowercase letters, number of capitals per character, number of lowercases per character, number of stopwords, number of punctuations, punctuation characters per character, number of words that are entirely in uppercase, number of words entirely in lowercase, number of words that are titled (start with captial letter, rest lowercase), number of characters per word, the number of sentences, the average length of a sentence in words, the maximum length of a sentence, the minimum length of a sentence, the standard deviation of sentence length, the number of repeated sentences, and whether or not the sentence contained a foreign word.
Olivier's features from
this kernel
:
whether the description starts with columns, has a timestamp, has a date, has a link, or has an email. I also added has IP address.
Parts of speech features:
My theory was that every insult, threat, etc. would have a unique part of speech expression, so I looked at the number of nouns, nouns per word, number of conjunctions, number of prepositions, number of adjectives, adjectives per word, number of modal words (e.g., should, will), number of personal pronouns, personal pronouns per word, number of adverbs, number of adverb participles, number of verbs, verbs per word, number of past tense verbs, number of third person singular present tense verbs, whether there is a modal followed by a verb (e.g., "should kill"), whether there is a personal pronoun followed by a singular present-tense verb (this captured things like "you bitch", since "bitch" was erroneously inferred to be a verb), whether there was an adjective followed by a noun, whether there was a noun followed by a preposition, whether there was a verb followed by the word "you" (e.g., "kill you"), and whether there was the word "you" followed by a verb (again, this would capture "you bitch").
Syllable-level data:
I thought that toxic comments would be much simpler than other comments, so I captured this with syllable-level data. I looked at the total number of syllables, the average syllables per word, the maximum number of syllables in a word, the standard deviation of syllables across words, the number of big words (more than two syllables), the number of simple words (one syllable), and number of big words per word.
Readability level:
Along the same lines as syllable info, I used some formal readability scores. I used
the two Flesch-Kincaid tests
,
SMOG grade
,
Linsear-Write grade
, the
Automated Readability Index
, and
the Gunning fog index
.
Manual bad word list:
I looked through
a bad word list
and
another one
for manual bad word features to highlight. I also took a look through our TFIDF vectorizers to see which bad words scored the worst. My partner then looked at the relative frequencies of every word to see what words occur the most in each label. We then manually binned these words into higher-level buckets (e.g., obscene words, threat words) and created higher-level features (e.g., has_obscene_word). The idea here was to try to help the model understand certain bad words with really low frequency by putting them into a bin.
AFINN scores:
I looked at
the AFINN sentiment scores
, and calculated the total AFINN score across all words in the comment, plus the mean AFFIN score on a word-by-word basis, the maximum AFINN score, the minimum AFINN score, the standard deviation of scores, the number of words with a score (instead of 0), the number of words with a positive score, the number of words with a negative score, the number of words with a score per word, the number of positive words per word, the number of negative words per word, and the ratio of positive to negative words.
Sentiment:
I also added the TextBlob sentiment polarity score.
My general approach here was to use a little bit of theory to guide what I was doing and pick features that felt sensible, whereas I would let TFIDF pick up whatever it wants. I manually tested the individual feature AUC of every feature to ensure that it had some signal… I dropped things that didn't score at least 0.55.
The feature engineering was against some tough competition competing with out of fold predictions, but I was pleased to see that when feature impact was run, a few of the custom features did beat out a good chunk of the models, and that deep trees were working for some of the labels and really using a lot of the features. Setting really low column sample rates helped a lot of these features shine and produce more diverse trees.
Level 1 Models
For the level 1 models, I did a whirlwind tour of the public kernels. I wouldn't be anywhere near where I was without these kernels, as no one on our team really understands neural nets. We had to use Google to even know what LSTM or GRU models were -- I'd never heard of them prior to the competition! For this competition, we used 53 different models:
16 different logistic regression models (112 features total).
I varied whether the model was trained with sag, with L1, with L2, or with
the naive bayes adjustment
. I varied the TFIDF matrix used, whether it was based on words (1-2 ngrams and 200K features), a cleaned word list (using
the preprocessing from this kernel
) with stopwords removed (1-2 ngrams and 200K features), based on characters (2-6 character grams and 200K features), or based on a combination of characters and words like
in this kernel
. The best model was a LR with the sag solver on the combination of characters and words, with a 5CV of 0.98587 on the original six labels. Each logistic regression was set up to produce seven labels, one for each of the original six and then a seventh "non-toxic" label that was 1 if all the labels were 0, or 0 otherwise. (I don't think the seventh label helped the final score that much.)
3 LightGBMs on TFIDF matricies (18 features total).
I used
my own LightGBM with SelectKBest approach
that did well for me in the Mercari competition. I trained one LightGBM on the word TFIDF matrix (1-2 ngrams and 200K features), another on the character TFIDF matrix (2-6 ngrams and 200K features) after
the preprocessing from this kernel
, and a third LightGBM on the union of character and word vectors (10K words and 50K characters, same as in the LR approach). Each feature set was reduced via SelectKBest and a Logistic Regression to about 10000 best features, as seen in my kernel. The part that I didn't include in my kernel that helped a lot was using dart boosting for the LightGBM and a 0.1 feature fraction, which allowed training for hundreds of rounds. The best model here was on the union TFIDF set, with a 5CV of 0.98468.
A LightGBM on the union TFIDF matrix plus all my feature engineering.
I took the same LightGBM from before and added my 423 additional features to it. This improved the 5CV score to 0.98779.
A LightGBM on the Twitter embedding, SVD, and all my feature engineering.
Rather than training the LightGBM on the TFIDF matrix and SelectKBest directly, I instead transformed the TFIDF matrix using the Twitter embedding (glove.twitter.27B.200d.txt) and using TruncatedSVD with 200 dimensions. I then added my 423 additional features to it from the custom feature engineering, for 823 features total. This made for my best non-NN single model, with a 5CV of 0.98788.
A factorization machine from
this kernel
.
I used it as-is but without the prediction chaining… I tried to add my own feature engineering to the bins, but it ended up overfitting quite badly. I also removed the prediction chaining because that was also overfitting for me. 5CV of 0.98730, but 0.9815 on the public leaderboard and 0.9813 on the private leaderboard.
A Ridge classifier
, loosely inspired by
this kernel
, but using the same features (and binning) as the factorization machine. 5CV of 0.98641, but 0.9813 on the public leaderboard and 0.9807 on the private leaderboard.
At this point, I was able to combine all my base models and feature engineering into a Level 2 LGB and get a 5CV of 0.98995, with 0.9848 on the public leaderboard. I knew the only way to go further would be to use neural nets, but I didn't understand them yet. So it was time to study up and go through the kernels. I used:
The Pooled GRU from
this kernel
.
5CV 0.98698.
A modified version of
that Pooled GRU
to use 200K max features (up from 30K), 200 max length (up from 100), and 0.3 spatial dropout instead of 0.2. I also used the Twitter-200d-27B embedding instead of Crawl-300d-2M and I used
Zafar's cleaned text
. This was all based on the theory I read in the discussion that higher max features, higher max length, and higher spatial dropout worked better, and the Twitter embedding was better, especially with a trainable embedding. This was my second best single model by 5CV, with a 5CV score of 0.98920, but it didn't do so well on the leaderboard, with a public leaderboard score of 0.9848 and a private leaderboard score of 0.9832.
Another modified version of
that Pooled GRU
with everything the same as in the kernel, but with Twitter-200d-27B embedding instead of Crawl-300d-2M, 0.5 spatial dropout instead of 0.2, and trained for an extra epoch (3 instead of 2). 5CV 0.98721.
The FastText GRU from
this kernel
.
5CV 0.98880, public leaderboard 0.9852, but private leaderboard 0.9839.
A modified version of
that FastText GRU
, with 200 max length instead of 175, Twitter-200d-27B embedding instead of Crawl-300d-2M, a trainable embedding, and
Zafar's cleaned text
. I had to drop the epochs down to 12 from 19. The 5CV showed improvement at 0.98972, making it my best single model. However, the public leaderboard and private leaderboard were worse at 0.9848 and 0.9832 respectively.
At this point I was having fun tweaking the kernels slightly and was amazed at how small tweaks could produce a new just as good model with a correlation of ~0.95. It seemed like each NN I was adding was producing a solid boost for my final ensemble, usually ~0.0002 or so. But I didn't really know what I was doing, so I dumped in more kernels. As long as the correlations were in check, it would give me more model diversity, which seemed like a good thing!
I used
the Bidirectional GRU from this kernel
(5CV 0.98623),
the double GRU from this kernel
(5CV 0.98646),
the 2DConv CNN from this kernel
(5CV 0.98807),
the Bi-LSTM from this kernel
(5CV 0.98863, Public Leaderboard 0.9846, Private Leaderboard 0.9836),
the DPCNN from this kernel
(5CV 0.98655),
the RNN+CNN from this kernel
(I rewrote it in Python) (5CV 0.98722),
the Capsule net from this kernel
(5CV 0.98358), and
the attention layer LSTM from this kernel
(5CV 0.98472).
Lastly, I played modify again and took the RNN+CNN and upped max features to 200K from 30K, maxlen to 200 from 100, used Twitter-200d-27B instead of glove.840B.300d, and swapped to a trainable embedding. The score increase was negligible (5CV 0.98722 -> 0.98725), but the result was surprisingly uncorrelated.
Some of the higher scorers noticed that different embeddings would be the key to model diversity. I didn't notice that, but I did realize it would be at least
somewhat
important, so I ended up with three different embeddings across the models -- Crawl-300d-2M, glove.840B.300d, and Twitter-200d-27B. I wonder if training more NNs on embeddings I didn't use would have upped my score.
At this point, adding more NNs was no longer increasing my ensemble score at all, so I stopped. Well, not quite. I did throw in
all the OOF predictions from the 16 models provided by Neptune
. This gave me some model diversity, as I think they trained some GPU-only models (whereas I couldn't figure out how to work a GPU) and trained some different embeddings (like fasttext).
Things I Tried that Didn't Work
In
the External Data thread
, I was surprised to learn that
the PerspectiveAPI was fair game
, so I painstakingly queried the ConvAI API for every row. It took 18 hours to run with the rate limit. However, it turned out that all the results were overfit, probably because the model was trained on the same train data as our data, so I couldn't get out of fold predictions.
I also tried to use the additional toxicity and aggression labels
as explored in this kernel
, but I noticed that the data was the same as in our train set but with different preprocessing, and I had trouble linking the data together. I trained a bunch of Ridge regressors on it, but the results would just overfit.
I explored a few different Level 2 and Level 3 architectures, where I stacked LightGBMs on top of each other and used the feature engineering more in the submodels, but it turned out that using all the feature engineering at the top level was both simpler and higher scoring.
I tried putting the Twitter embeddings and 200-dimension SVM on the second level tree models, but it looked like it was overfitting and the overall dataset ballooned too large (2.4GB) to effectively tune.
I couldn't get any worthwhile SVM model to work.
Things I Wish I Had More Time to Explore
It would have been nice to know more about the various NNs and how to build and tune them. I was mildly successful at making my own NNs with better 5CV scores and good model correlation, but I couldn't improve upon the kernels in the leaderboard and emphatically did not know what I was doing. Seeing
the best single model private leadearboard scores
, my single models had a lot of room to improve. My best private leaderboard score for a single model was a GRU with private leaderboard 0.9841, which is a far cry from the 0.986X's being reported by some. Unfortunately, I just don't know yet how to make a GRU good, and I'm not exactly sure where to learn.
If I had more time, I would have explored dropping some of the features or submodels to see if that improved the model scores, or maybe even made specific feature sets unique for each label.
This is a bit rough since the competition scores were so close, I feel like exploring any one thing could have been enough to send us flying up a few ranks.
Another idea my teammate had that we're not sure is any good is repetitively resampling and augmenting the data set with the mislabeled / borderline toxic comments. The high AUC seems mostly driven by very easy to identify good comments and we wonder if removing the bulk of them will reduce some of the overfitting on the “good” side (probably not).
Things I Think About With The Benefit of Hindsight
In hindsight, I should have explored training on a wider variety of embeddings. I never thought about byte encoding embeddings or combining embeddings, or just being systematic about training with a bunch of different embeddings. I also wonder how training different embeddings with LightGBM would have helped.
I initially thought about using the translation augmentation approach, but didn't think it would be that important and didn't have time to explore it. Seeing it being used by the highest ranked people makes me really wish I had more time to explore this.
I was too nervous about pseudo-labeling the test set and worried that it would overfit, so I didn't do it. I should have at least explored it and seen how it changed the 5CV and leaderboard scores. If it increased both substantially, I could have convinced myself to use it for at least one of my two submissions. …But I didn't look into it. In hindsight, another mistake. Given how useful pseudo-labeling was, I wonder if it would have been useful to pseudo-label more of the Wikipedia comment dumps that were not in the train or test set.
Key Takeaways
I don't have to understand NNs to get a good score with them, but I'll probably need to understand them to get a gold medal someday.
Kernels are great. I checked kernels every day and still ended up missing some stuff!
It seems like taking almost every single public kernel, training them with 5CV, combining them with a little bit of special secret sauce and a good level 2 stacking scheme, is enough to do well at Kaggle.
Even slight tweaks to NNs can produce new models with low (~0.95) correlations.
Variety in embeddings is important for model diversity.
Varying input data is just as important, if not more important, than varying the model being used.
Pseduo-labeling and train/test augmentation can work.
Models that are weak on level 1 can be the best contributors to level 2, and models that are weak on level 2 can still be the best contributors to level 3.
Feature engineering can be really useful.
DART mode on LightGBM can be really useful.
Code
The complete code for the solution can be found here:
https://github.com/peterhurford/kaggle-toxic_comment
Everything (including the NNs) was trained on an Amazon c5.9xlarge. The total runtime of all the files should be under a day. Nearly all the models execute five folds in under 20 minutes per fold, with the exception of a few of the NNs.
Thanks
In conclusion, thanks to everyone who shared their kernels. I was really impressed by how forthcoming everyone was in discussing their solutions. I'd be way down the leaderboard without you. Special shoutouts to Zafar, Olivier, Bojan, Tilli, and Yekenot. I'll endeavor to share more of my approach in kernels in future competitions to pay this forward.
Also thanks to Jigsaw for providing such an interesting competition. I've never seen AUCs in the >0.9 range before, so that was fun to play with. Also thanks for gracefully handling pretty much every possible way the competition could fail.
Ultimately, despite the difference in train and test, the competition ended up being pretty straightforward. Unlike for Porto Seguro, my CV mostly lined up with the Public and Private leaderboards, and I was able to successfully pick my two best private leaderboard submissions as my two submissions.

title: Mercari Price Suggestion Challenge: Can you automatically suggest product prices to online sellers?
introduction:
== Description ===
It can be hard to know how much something’s really worth. Small details can mean big differences in pricing. For example, one of these sweaters cost $335 and the other cost $9.99. Can you guess which one’s which?
Product pricing gets even harder at scale, considering just how many products are sold online. Clothing has strong seasonal pricing trends and is heavily influenced by brand names, while electronics have fluctuating prices based on product specs.
Mercari
, Japan’s biggest community-powered shopping app, knows this problem deeply. They’d like to offer pricing suggestions to sellers, but this is tough because their sellers are enabled to put just about anything, or any bundle of things, on Mercari's marketplace.
In this competition, Mercari’s challenging you to build an algorithm that automatically suggests the right product prices. You’ll be provided user-inputted text descriptions of their products, including details like product category name, brand name, and item condition.
Note that, because of the public nature of this data, this competition is a “Kernels Only” competition. In the second stage of the challenge, files will only be available through Kernels and you will not be able to modify your approach in response to new data. Read more details in the
data tab
and
Kernels FAQ page
.

solutions.1st place:
Hello everyone, thanks for an amazing competition. Together with Konstantin we are very excited, probably too much to describe our solution in greater detail - tomorrow we will write more.
However we have something to whet your appetites. Konstantin did an amazing job and created a very small kernel based on our work over those 3 months that achieves 0.3875 on the validation … and it is only 83 LOC - how cool is that!
https://www.kaggle.com/lopuhin/mercari-golf-0-3875-cv-in-75-loc-1900-s
UPDATE 2
Link to solution
https://github.com/pjankiewicz/mercari-solution
~
~~ UPDATE
~
~~
Full description
Pawel’s premerge solution (~0.3950)
I had a pretty complicated models before teaming up with Konstantin. It consisted of 3 parts:
Models per category - I created ridge models for category level 1, 2, 3, combinations of category 2 + shipping and item_condition_id etc. They were quite fast to train and created 0.4050 solution in about 20 minutes.
Residual models MLP - based on the 1. models I trained next models on sparse inputs (neural networks). The target was the difference between the predictions and real prices (think of a boosting but with strong models).
Residual model LGBM - the same idea as 2.
While the concept of training models per category seems like a good one it is really not. Training models like this is cool but it underestimates the model one is using. You can think that a neural network can’t be trained to understand the interaction between categories and descriptions, brands etc. This is a wrong assumption. Our example shows that a single well tuned neural network can learn what it wants.
Konstantin’s premerge solution. (~0.3920)
Before the merge, I had two base models:
Sparse MLP implemented in Tensorflow, without any sophisticated features, compared to public kernels I tweaked only the number of features, and tokenizer using eli5 explanations of the Ridge model. 3 models were trained sequentially.
CNN with conv1d, similar to what was in many kernels, implemented in Keras. The model itself was not great, but it was very different from an MLP model, so gave a nice boost.
The merge
At the moment of merging Konstantin was first and I was second. Someone would say “why did we merge at all”. But we did and it was a good decision. We expected that in order to succeed it wasn’t enough to blindly merge 2 solutions. In fact we had to create 1 solution which uses ideas of both of us. Making it work under the constraints was very challenging. The time wasn’t such a big deal for us, we focused more on the memory and being able to run 4 neural networks at the same time.
It took us maybe 2 weeks to come up with a unified solution (probably we worked the hardest at that point). It turned out that 2 different preprocessing schemes (2 datasets) created much needed variance in the solutions and we easily improved by 0.01 which was quite a big jump.
In the end we used 3 datasets and 4 models in each dataset. We tried to diversify the models:
different tokenization, with/without stemming
countvectorizer / tfidfvectorizer
Build system
It was quite impossible to manage this project without a way to split our solution into modules. We independently created a build system for our code. Eventually we used the system that created a Python package with the solution. Our script was strange and looked like this (pseudocode):
ENCODED_FILES = {
some
base64 encoded characters}
DECODE_FILES 
INSTALL THE MERCARI
PACKAGE
RUN MAIN FUNCTIONS
content_copy
It was really important to run models in 3 sequential processes because Python has a tendency not to clean the memory after some operations (especially data preprocessing).
Feature preprocessing
Some tricks/no-tricks that worked:
name chargrams - We don’t know why exactly but using character n-grams from name improved the score. Maybe it was because it produced relatively dense features
stemming - we used a standard PorterStemmer
numerical vectorization - we noticed that a very big source of errors were bundle items with descriptions like: “10 data 5 scientists” were vectorized to data=10, scientists=5. This vectorizer applied in only 1 dataset improved the ensemble by 0.001. We didn’t have much time to test this idea further.
text concatenation - to reduce the dimensionality of the text fields by just concatenating them together - we tested all configurations {name, item_description, category, brand}. This was a reason for the 0.37xx push.
Whatever cool idea we had about additional feature engineering didn’t work. To name a few:
Extraction of features like “for [Name]”. We noticed that many items were designated to a particular person. We weren’t sure what it meant exactly but it seemed important enough to create a feature. We created a list of names from nltk and searched for similar strings with AhoCorasick algorithm.
We noticed that there were issues with new lines in descriptions. Wherever someone used a newline in description it concatenated the words likethis.
Spell checking.
Quoting Pawel:
neural networks are like "ok I guess I can use your
feature engineering
here you are 0.0003 increase"
Models
Pawel discovered that with a properly tuned sparse MLP model, it’s better to achieve diversity in the ensemble by training the same model on different datasets, compared to different models on the same dataset. So we decided to stick to one model, which really simplified our solution. The base model is a multilayer feedforward neural network with sparse inputs: nothing fancy at all, so it’s surprising it works so well. I think one reason is that it’s more efficient compared to other approaches: the dataset is large, so the model must have big capacity and be able to capture feature interactions. But in the time that a conv1d CNN could train on 4 cores with embedding size 32, we could train 4 MLP models with hidden size 256.
Careful learning schedule tuning is crucial: most importantly, we doubled batch size after each epoch, which made the model train faster after each epoch and also lead to better final performance. We also lowered the learning rate in addition to batch size increase. Everything was tuned to get the best validation score after the second epoch, and then overfit after the third epoch: this made the model much stronger in the ensemble.
Compared to the model in the kernel (
https://www.kaggle.com/lopuhin/mercari-golf-0-3875-cv-in-75-loc-1900-s)
, we had some extra tweaks:
We had two model variations that we used: one was trained with Huber loss (it’s better here as it’s less sensitive to outliers), and another was doing classification instead of regression. For classification, we split all prices into 64 buckets, and created a soft target for prediction: first calculate L2 distance from the centers of the buckets, and then apply softmax to this (with high softmax temperature which was a hyperparameter). This classification model achieved better score on it’s own due to less overfitting, and also added diversity.
For 2 out of 4 models for each dataset, we binarized input data during training and prediction by setting all non-zero values to 1. This is like getting an extra dataset with a binary CountVectorizer instead of TFIDF for free. I think it’s a great idea, kudos to Pawel! We also tried to binarize using non-zero thresholds, but this didn’t bring much improvement.
L2 regularization helped a little (we applied it only to the first layer), also Tensorflow models worked better with PRELU activations instead of RELU.
Model implementation and optimization: as it’s a kernel competition with very hard constraints for this dataset size, it was important to make training maximally efficient: by making the first hidden layer bigger, it was possible to improve the score, and we also had 12 models to train in addition to preparing dataset. In the end, we managed to train 12 models with hidden size 256 on about 200k features. Here is how we did it:
TF can use multiple cores, but it’s very far from linear scaling, especially for sparse models. So it is better to use one core for each model and train 4 models in parallel: we restricted TF to one core with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 and usual TF config variables, and then allowed TF to use multiple cores with threading using undocumented use_per_session_threads=1: this meant that we didn’t need to start multiple processes and used less memory.
It turns out that MXNet allows for a more efficient CPU implementation of a sparse MLP, because it has support for sparse updates (maybe TF has it too, but we were not able to use it). Pawel wrote an initial MXNet version that was about 2x faster, and then we added all features from TF models and made it work even better. The problem was that MXNet executor engine is not thread safe, if you try to parallelize using threading you get either 1 core used, or segfault. So we had to move to multiprocessing and to also write our own data generator because MXNet one made a lot of copies and used too much memory. We also had a version with putting data into shared memory, but it was way too close to disk space limit, so we had to scratch that.
Overall MXNet solution was faster and allowed to use a smaller initial batch size without loss in speed, but used more memory and looked less reliable. So at the end we had two submissions using the same datasets, one with MXNet (0.37758 private LB / 0.37665 public), and one with TF (0.38006 private / 0.37920 public).
At the end, we had 12 predictions and needed to merge them. An average worked well, but it was better to tune blending weights, so we used 1% of the dataset for validation (5% locally) and tuned the weights using a Lasso model. Lasso uses L1 regularization, so it was a bit funny when you have some idea and add more models, but Lasso says: meh, I don’t want your new models, and sets their weights to zero.
Models that did not work:
MoE (mixture of experts): this is a really cool paper
https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538
which describes how to train a model which has more capacity while using the same compute budget: exactly what we want here! But at the end it turned out that TF lacks sparse support for some operations required to make it work.
We tried to add some exotic model blends for example: merging FM and MLP in the same architecture, adding a skip layer with linear regression to the output of MLP. It all eventually converged to a simple MLP.
We achieved a point where only ways to improve was to train bigger MLP networks but due to constraints we couldn’t. This was really evident because models improved only when we added more data/features to the ensemble.
Meta Statistics
Slack messages: 4500
Git commits: 152 (317 across all branches)
PR merged: 31
Python LOC: 2015
solutions.2nd place:
So here's our second place solution (the kernel we are publishing is almost similar to the winning kernel)
The kernel scored 0.38888 on public and 0.38948 on private and run in 2800s
https://www.kaggle.com/mchahhou/second-place-solution
As a preprocessing step, we kept maximum 60 words for all names and descriptions and apply the same cleaning process on all the texts
We  labelEncoded all brand and categories and concatenated the encoded values with the name feature
We made 4 models :
1) Ridge model : trained on 1-ngrams and custom bigrams.
1-ngrams is using both name and description. Our custom bigrams work as follows :  we concatenate name with the first 5 words from description,  then apply np.unique() on the list of word to sort them and remove duplicates,  then create all 2-way possible combination of words.
The ridge model is able to score .418 on public LB
2) Sparse NN model trained on a CountVectorizer with ngram_range=(1,2). The NN is fit with sparse data from name and description features
3) a fastText NN model with a shared_embedding layer for name and description features
4) another Sparse NN model fit with character Ngrams using name and description features.
We waste half our time building an LGB model that didnt help even though it was our best model. We found that using different models with the same data representation is not going to work. We then choose to use different NN with different inputs
To make our NN fast, we double the batch size after each epoch. This is quite similar to reducing the learning rate after each epoch with the advantage of speed gain

**Our kernel is here:
https://www.kaggle.com/peterhurford/lgb-and-fm-18th-place-0-40604**
When DataGeek and I merged, we were surprised to see we both had roughly the same solution (LGB and FM average with similar LGB architectures), so we tried to combine the best features from each of our approaches. The general idea was building a LGB on all the categorical data and using Ridge models as variables in the LGB to represent the text data. We did 2-fold CV to get out-of-fold predictions to use in the LGB. We also did a lot of feature engineering for both the FM and LGB to learn what the TFIDF and Wordbatch would not learn, which is things like spacing, punctuation, ratios, etc.
Two great boosts to our model included using a Multinominal Naive Bayes submodel in the LGB to correct for the tendency of the Ridge models to underestimate and a
SelectKBest
and a regression to find the top performing individual wordbatch vectors and included them in our LGB. Both of these tricks improved our position by ~0.003 each.
Overall, our LGB had 48000 individual wordbatch vectors found via
SelectKBest
and a regression; 37 custom feature engineering variables made and tested by hand; target encoded versions of brand, category 1, category 2, category 3, and the first word of the item description; and 4 2-fold submodels (one Ridge trained on everything, one MNB trained on everything, one Ridge trained on just the name vectors, and one Ridge trained on just the item description vectors). We tried running the FM as a submodel in the LGB also, but it ended up surprisingly more valuable as a standalone model that we would average with.
We had a big scramble at the end to get Stage 2 ready (definitely should've started preparing for that earlier!) and took a 0.005 drop from our best non-ready submission. We ended up submitted two different approaches -- one with batched predictions and one with not. I would like to share my approach with you. First of all big thanks to the competition hosts for my first Kaggle experience and congrats to the winners. I had a lot of fun and learned many new things!
My approach was to use an ensemble of five RNN's, each consisting of two parallel GRU-Cells. I assumed that the intrinsic properties of the unit cell for both energies are different and therefore require two seperate representations. Each RNN output tensor was averaged in time, concatenated and then fed into a three-layer MLP with ReLU activations. I appended a visualization of the network architecture.
Each network was trained with MSE as objective function, Adam optimizer and gradient clipping. The final predictions were weighted by a linear regression model.
As RNN's are very data hungry I also used data augmentation to artifically increase the size of the dataset. I rotated the atomic coordinates by using rotation matrices with different angles in the range of 45° to 315°. This was driven by the assumption that the intrinsic properties are invariant to linear transformations. Best results were given by choosing 7 equidistant angles. I also found that too much data augmentation performed worse. This approach led to a significant increase of ~0.01 in CV- and LB-score.
Thank you and have a nice weekend!
Edit:
Training the networks took approx. 1 - 1.5 hours. This is due to the fast Keras CuDNNGRU implementation.
The elements as one-hot-encoded vectors were concatenated to the corresponding position vectors. Lattice vectors were concatenated in front of the atomic position matrix and the resulting matrix zero padded to a shape of 80 x 7 . As a physicist by training, I of course had to participate in this competition. But it turned out that detailed knowledge of physics was not necessary at all, just some basic 3 dimensional geometry.
What didn't work:
First I tried to actually calculate the band gaps and the formation energies with density functional theory (using the ase and gpaw python packages). Because of limited resources, I could only spend a few minutes of CPU time on each crystal. So in the end the accuracy of the solutions was not good enough, although there was a clear correlation between the results and the target variables.
What did work:
My idea then was to construct features which better describe the geometry of the crystals in a coordinate system independent way. So I first made 80 new features that encode the radial density distributions of the atoms as described in
https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.1266
. However, this approach throws away all information about angles. So I made 80 additional features that encode the angular distributions of the atoms that are closest to each other.
For the machine learning model I used xgboost. I noticed that the log error for the formation energy was always much lower than for the band gap. So I first predicted the formation energies, and used the predictions as an additional feature when predicting the band gap.
My local CV score was 0.049, and my public leaderboard score was 0.0515. I was only at the 253rd position on the public data, so I was very pleasantly surprised that I finished on 9th place in the private leaderboard! I guess that the 100 test data points for the public leaderboard data were really not enough for a reliable estimate of the quality of the model, and I got a bit unlucky there.
Anyway, it was a fun competition, but too bad that there are no medals awarded…

I and my colleague Kareem have computer engineering background and our colleague Mohamed have bioinformatics background. Since we lack the domain knowledge of material science, we decided to work with deep learning models.

Voxnet [1]: in which we divided the space to small equally sized voxels and constructed a 3d matrix for each material. In each voxel, we counted the number of atoms located in it. Pointnet [2]: in which we described point-wise features (xyz position, one hot encoding of atom type, molecular weight, count of adjacent atoms and bond valence), then used pointnet model which is basically a series of 1d convolution layers followed by max-pooling as aggregation function and lastly some feed forward layers. In both models we added the precomputed features by the organizers in the last feed forward layers. For cross validation, we used 24 folds.
Our selected submission is an ensemble of multiple versions of point net and voxel net with different number of layers and filters, and some xgboost models with distance and position based features. This submission had a cv score of 0.0464 and private lb score of 0.0573.

introduction:
== Description ===
Finding footage of a crime caught on tape is an investigator's dream. But even with crystal clear, damning evidence, one critical question always remains–is the footage real?
Today, one way to help authenticate footage is to identify the camera that the image was taken with. Forgeries often require splicing together content from two different cameras. But, unfortunately, the most common way to do this now is using image metadata, which can be easily falsified itself.
This problem is actively studied by several researchers around the world. Many machine learning solutions have been proposed in the past: least-squares estimates of a camera's color demosaicing filters as classification features, co-occurrences of pixel value prediction errors as features that are passed to sophisticated ensemble classifiers, and using CNNs to learn camera model identification features. However, this is a problem yet to be sufficiently solved.
For this competition, the IEEE Signal Processing Society is challenging you to build an algorithm that  identifies which camera model captured an image by using traces intrinsically left in the image. Helping to solve this problem would have a big impact on the verification of evidence used in criminal and civil trials and even news reporting.

Averaging all TTA prediction from all models by power mean - powers of 1,2,4 as a parameter. Additionally, we explicitly made all classes equally distributed (132 manip and 132 unalt photos for each class) by using Hungarian algorithm on probabilities. As expected, this resulted in a huge LB overfit: 0.991 score on public and 0.985 on private.
Blending models by using hold-out predictions. There were 52 models with slightly different parameters and equal weights: XGBoost (20) + LightGBM (20) + Keras (12). No class equalization was used with this approach except some weight tuning for Nexus 5 during training (all models had a smaller number of predictions for this phone).

Collect as much data as possible but do not forget to clean it (GIGO)
Try smaller crops first and all architecture types
LB probing is evil, trust your CV

Data
The training set has been augmented with both private images and images downloaded from Flickr.
All images were preliminary sifted based on the EXIF header meta-data information,
to keep only images with meta-data coherent with the corresponding camera of the training set.
All images that were processed by an editing software or with restrictive license were removed.
Finally we obtained a dataset of 450 images per model (about 15 GB). 400 images have been used for training, 50 images for validation.
Training
During training patches were randomly extracted from the central part of image (1024x1024 pixels) and randomly rotated with steps of 90 degrees.
We trained separate networks for the model identification of unaltered and manipulated images.
For the first problem, we included only unaltered images in the training set.
On the contrary, the networks for manipulated images were trained using both unaltered and manipulated images, as we found this solution to provide consistently better results.
Solution overview
Fusion of different CNNs models (arithmetic mean of the scores).
For unaltered images we considered 5 networks trained at different patch size: XceptionNet (96), XceptionNet (299), Inception v3 (139), InceptionResNet v2 (299), DenseNet121 (224).
For manipulated images we considered the same networks above but used various input patch sizes, for a total of 14 models.
We tested many alternative solutions to improve performance, two of them were eventually applied: 1) network training on small patches and fine-tuning on larger ones, 2) identification of problematic classes (JPEG 70 and Resizing 0.5) and design of dedicated detectors.
Hardware
NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU with 16GB of RAM.
Special mention
It is interesting that using only a single model for unaltered (XceptionNet on patches of dimension 96) and manipulated images (XceptionNet on patches of dimension 96 fine tuned on 299) gave a public score = 0.986666 and a private score = 0.981309.
Lessons learnt
Do not trust the public LB too much. Use a better validation set!

Here is a brief summary of my steps.
Edit: I only used the central 80% crop of the train data because the boundaries are often statistically very different from the test data. For example, if the original image size is 1000x1000, only the central 800x800 crop is used. This center-cropping applies to train data only, and it gave around 1% higher accuracy than training on the original size.
Finetune a pretrained inception_v3 with random 480x480 crops. The provided training set and Gleb's data were used. My data augmentation include the eight possible manipulations but no transpose, rotation or flipping as I believe they should not help in theory. JPEG compression is always aligned (the 8x8 grid) as I bet re-compressions were done before cropping. This achieved Public LB 0.976 and Private LB 0.972.
Predict the test set ('unalt' images only) using the finetuned model. Use the predicted probabilities as pseudo-labels for test data and merge the test data with the training set.  Continue tuning with the merged set. After the pseudo-labeling, the performance improved to Public LB 0.983 and Private LB 0.976.
Group the 'unalt' images in test set by predicted labels and estimate the sensor noise patterns for each camera in test set (totally ten reference patterns). Then match each of the 'unalt' images with the ten reference patterns, and correct the predictions when the correlation between an image and a reference pattern is larger than a certain threshold. I also corrected the 'manip' part by matching their sensor noises with the augmented (by the eight manipulations) reference patterns. The last step gave the largest boost: Public LB 0.986 and Private LB 0.987.
Thanks to Kaggle and IEEE SPS for hosting this interesting competition.
Thanks to everyone who generously shared their data and ideas.

Here is a brief overview of our modeling and solution. Please feel free to ask any questions.
We only used the data provided by Kaggle and Gleb´s links. We had some concerns about the Gleb's dataset license of use for some of the images, to be honest, but most of them seem to be good.
We first tried some CNN models from scratch, but discovered that the well known pretrained models converge faster and gave better accuracy. Our best single model was a DenseNet201 trained  on patches of size 336x336 scoring 0.963/0.967 (public/private LB). As the accuracy was pretty high, we decide to give a try to pseudo-labeled images from the testset using the predictions from this model.
We applied a threshold of p>=0.999 and used only unaltered images. This gives us 1116 new images to train with.
The same DenseNet201 model, trained now with this extra dataset, scored 0.975/0.973. After intense TTA, it gave us 0.980/0.975.
We trained a few more models (another DenseNet201, InceptionResnetV2, etc.) , but we couldn't improve much by just blending their predictions (and also being worried about overfitting to the LB), we decide to try stacking predictions from different models, and to train a second layer model with them.
Since we only had about a week to train them, and since we didn't have too many GPU resources, we decided to do stacking with just 2-folds.
While we were training NN models, we tried to extract image features to train a non-NN model. We basically followed the ideas from this paper:
"Using sensor pattern noise for camera model identification" Thomas Filler, Jessica Fridrich, Miroslav Goljan
We extracted approx. 3000 features from image linear pattern and noise pattern. We trained XGB, LightGBM and MultilayerPerceptron after applying PCA, scoring 0.898/0.881. (We found out that PCA reduced the training times of the models, but the raw dataset was trainable as well, achieving similar performance, if not better.)
Our final model is an XGB model of stacked predictions from 9 L1 models:
- From images: DenseNet201, VGG16, Xception, DenseNet121, InceptionV3, ResNet50 (we tried others but we discarded them)
- From extracted features: XGB, LightGBM, MultilayerPerceptron
This model (A13) scored 0.9877/0.9866. We trained the same model but excluding pseudolabeled data. We thought that they could introduce a strong bias toward these images, and after all, they were already used for all ours L1 models. This second model (A13a) scored  0.9798/0.9847, and we made the random decision of select this submission for the final, finishing 10th instead of 5th. (Our 2nd final submissions was a optimized weighted average of several submissions scoring 0.9885/0.9835, but we weren't very confident about it).

solutions.7th place:
As has been widely discussed, I had trouble with CV schemes, engineered features, and with how to use the reservation data.  In the end i built many models based on a variety of ways for treating both of these.
For timed-based CV I used 6-week blocks starting at week 14 of the data.  So I trained on weeks 1-13, evaluated on weeks 14-19;  trained on weeks 1-20, evaluated on weeks 21-26, etc.  This gave me a fold that had a golden week .  Doing this meant I had sets of training data developed only on what preceded the evaluation fold.  But then I also used a random 5-fold CV for some models.
For the reservation data, I ended up using it "indirectly".  I calculated the standard deviation of the reservation counts and reservation visitors per store for things like each city & weekday, or each genre and weekday, or each ward, etc.  I used these to calculate an "expected visitor" number for each store based on the store's mean/stdev visitors, but using the std of the reservation counts or reservation visitors.  So if the store was in city X and that city had a stdev of 1.5, I got a expected visitors for every store in city X using (store mean visitors)+1.5(store stdev visitors).  For a single expected visitors value I averaged all of the estimates for each store.  The reservation count (i.e. number of reservations for a day) ended up being a better estimator than the reservation visitors.
Engineered Features.  I didn't use very many.  The best ones were: Reservation-based expected visitors Rolling averages (I used a simple linear interpolation to fill in missing days).  I also used these for an LSTM that didn't work out so well. Store competitor counts.  So store counts with similar genres that were within 1 mile, or within "walking distance" (800 meters) I also set my "golden_week" flag to 1 during the Christmas week.
Target feature.  My weekday rolling averages, after adjusting for holidays, was an almost overpowering feature in LGBM and XGB so for a couple models I changed the target feature to be visitors-the rolling average.  That really mixed up feature importances, and performed a bit worse than the visitor-target, but good enough to include in my ensembling.
Ensemble.  I used a Neural Network (one hidden layer) to combine the various models.
Thanks for reading through all that!  That solution didn't fair so well.  Because I lost the last two lottery competitions by sticking with my CV, I decided I had better choose an "overfit the public LB" model just in case.  So I averaged the .479 SurpriseMe!  with my best single public LB model, that used a 5-fold CV, and built all features using all of the training data (future included).  And that model got me 7th place :-)

Basic model idea
content_copy
Based on lightgbm (best library in 2018 for liberaly throwing in data), treated the problem as a time series problem.
I made two submissions, one was a simpler version, and one was complex ensembled variation using the same features.
The simple version was a weekly model, which means I had 5 models in total.
I also had a daily model for week2. The reason is that the number of reserve decays exponentially (see above image), so the reserve data is important on closer-to-public-leaderboard days.
In the complex version, I trained stores that have data before 2016-03-01 (about 300/820 of the stores do) separately.

Thank you for my teammate Taka, Kaggle Admin, Recruit company, and all participants of this exciting competition. We would like to share our 20th solution, which is based on target encoding, customized sample_weight, data imputation and augmentation.
1. Problem setting
We were required to predict Japanese restaurants visitors from the restaurants' attribute information and historical information. Although the training data covers the dates from 2016 until April 2017, most of the stores are not observed January 2016. In terrible case, its first observation is March 2017, which is just before the test period.
2. Validation method
We split the last one month of the train data as validation set before conducting any feature engineering. The validation set was split to first 6 days as pseudo-Public and the rest as pseudo-Private. This method was really important for avoiding overfitting to Public Leaderboard and to know genuine performance of our models.
3. Feature engineering
We mainly conducted two feature engineering methods. One is target encodings and the other is creation of weather-based features. In addition, we used some ideas from public kernel carefully.
a. Target encodings
We conducted target encodings with combinations of "attribute information of the store" and "time-based features". Various statistics were created by this encoding as below.
attribute information of the store
air_store_id, air_genre_name, air_area_name, prefecture
time-based features
year, month, day, day_of_week, is_holiday (including Sat and Sun), is_yesterday_holiday, is_tomorrow_holiday, rolling mean of is_holiday (forward), rolling mean of is_holiday (backward) etc.
statistics
mean, min, max, sum, var
b. Weather features
Daily weather (precipitation, daylight, temperature)
Inner product of "hourly weather vector" and "hourly visitor vector".
Getting sick index, which is distance from optimal temperature and humidity for virus. We conducted 7 day rolling mean of the index considering virus latency period. This feature was more effective than we expected.
4. Sample weight
We designed the sample weight as the sum of two sample_weights (a + 0.3*b) considering the importance of recent events and annual periodicity. All parameters such as half-life was determined experimentally by validation scores. For validation and test, we used sample_weights with different values produced by the same logic, rather than sample_weights with same values.
a. Exponentially decayed weight (sample_weight_a)
We created an exponentially decayed weight with half-life of 60 days.
b. similarity-based weight (sample_weight_b)
We defined similarity of each months to the target period as predictability by LightGBM.
Fig 1. Customized sample_weight designed as sum of two components
5. Data imputation and augmentation
a. Imputation
Although month-based engineered features were really effective for public and pseudo-public score, it caused a catastrophic result to the pseudo-private score. Therefore, we imputed missing values of these statistics of May by ensemble of various regressors. We used the attribute features of the stores and the trend of 2016 as training data and these of 2017 as test data for this imputation.
b. Augmentation
Our hypothesis is that the first observation date of the stores is simply date of registration and not date of grand opening. Therefore, it is arbitrary decision by store owner and it should not change the visitors substantially. Based on this hypothesis, we randomly dropped past observation of both of train and test data. After that, obtained predictions were averaged. We expected that this processing increases the number of training data and make our model more robust. It should be noted that this processing is different from simple subsample because target encoding is conducted after augmentation and it brings change to created features.
Fig 2. Stochastic drop of past observations as data augmentation
6. Result
20th/2158.

title: Statoil/C-CORE Iceberg Classifier Challenge: Ship or iceberg, can you decide from space?
introduction:
== Description ===
Drifting icebergs present threats to navigation and activities in areas such as offshore of the East Coast of Canada.
Currently, many institutions and companies use aerial reconnaissance and shore-based support to monitor environmental conditions and assess risks from icebergs.  However, in remote areas with particularly harsh weather, these methods are not feasible, and the only viable monitoring option is via satellite.
Statoil
, an international energy company operating worldwide, has worked closely with companies like
C-CORE
. C-CORE have been using satellite data for over 30 years and have built a computer vision based surveillance system. To keep operations safe and efficient, Statoil is interested in getting a fresh new perspective on how to use machine learning to more accurately detect and discriminate against threatening icebergs as early as possible.
In this competition, you’re challenged to build an algorithm that automatically identifies if a remotely sensed target is a ship or iceberg. Improvements made will help drive the costs down for maintaining safe working conditions.

== Evaluation ===
Submissions are evaluated on the
log loss
between the predicted values and the ground truth.
Submission File
For each id in the test set, you must predict the probability that the image contains an iceberg (a number between 0 and 1). The file should contain a header and have the following format:
id,is_iceberg
809385f7,0.5
7535f0cd,0.4
3aa99a38,0.9

solutions.1st place:
We’d like to thank Kaggle and the competition sponsors for hosting this exciting competition.  The manageable size of the dataset as well as the technical challenge of working with satellite imagery kept us motivated to work on this problem.
I’d like to thank my partner Weimin for being such a great collaborator on this problem.  This was a great example of two people coming together with diverse solutions and combining for a gain we wouldn’t have achieved individually.
On to the solution…
Key findings/learnings:
Following first principles of visualizing and generating an
understanding the data were key. Visualizing inc_angle was the key
finding that led us down our solution path.
inc_angle pattern –   inc_angle’s with identical values (out to 4
decimal places) had the    same label 97% of the time.
There were two distinct groups that once separated can be treated
separately with individual models. inc_angle clusters show unique
alternating pattern of pure iceberg’s 100% of the time in train.
Let’s call this group1.  The non-group1 inc_angles have a pattern of
dense iceberg’s in the center and more ships just outside the center
of the distributions.  Call these group2.
This plot below is just a slice of a simple distribution plot of the individual train data by inc_angle.  The plot on the left is the raw training data, the plot on the right is also the training data but from one of our CV’s.  Notice the alternating patterns of natural groups.  These patterns propagate through the entire distribution of inc_angle and can be identified by basic clustering algorithm.  Ward’s, KNN, and density based clustering were among the types we used.
image
https://kaggle2.blob.core.windows.net/forum-message-attachments/273702/8369/inc_angle%20plot_small.jpg
•    Log_loss is a very unforgiving metric.  When using clustering and predicting on different groups it’s important to understand the group probability in addition to the individual point probability and threshold the risk appropriately.  We stayed away from extreme values.  We also didn’t trust the leaderboard too much given the sensitivity of log_loss and the fact only 20% of a relatively small dataset being reported on the public LB.  We relied on CV as our main form of feedback.
Solution overview:
We started with a CNN pipeline of 100+ diverse models which included architectures such as customized CNNs, VGG, mini-GoogLeNet, several different Densenet variations, and others.  Some of these included inc_angle after the fully connected layers and others didn’t.
We then ensembled and stacked the results and ran the predictions through a post-processing pipeline to transfer the signal from like inc_angles, although since not all like inc_angles had the same label we applied a max threshold by which the prediction could from the original prediction and if this threshold was exceeded we kept the original prediction.  From there we ran a clustering algorithm to identify the group1 and group2 inc_angle distributions.  Since
100%
group1 labels from train were icebergs, we applied a threshold of this to test.  There were 897 of these points in the test set and it appears from private LB score variants we have they were indeed all icebergs in test.
We then re-trained the 100+ CNN models on those
group2 training samples only
.  This appears to be the biggest difference in our approach and other top solutions so far and showed a significant improvement in ship detection as it gave us better signal to noise.  This group was then ensembled/stacked and concatenated with the original clustering (trained on all data).  We then fed this result into a post processing pipeline which ran various clustering algorithms on the result to identify dense regions of like predictions.  Each clustering algorithm used its own unique threshold/clipping value determined by CV.  The group1 and group2 results were then combined for the final prediction.
So in summary, 200+ CNN models, a handful of clustering algorithms, a few different thresholds, a heavy reliance on inc_angle, don’t push log_loss thresholds to the extreme, trust your local CV, and you have a formula for a winning solution.  Cheers!

solutions.4th place:
Thanks to everyone for the competition! Our 'best submission' gave score '0.0854' on the private leaderboard, but wasn't selected by us as the score on the public leaderboard was '0.0951'. From the final results one can see that there was a minor shake up within people who stayed on the top, so my guess is it was really hard to be sure about which submission is the best, either due to the size of the training data or outliers in the test set.
Our final solution looks as follows:
Train 5 NNs on image data (excluding incidence angle). Each model is using CV5 with the same split. NN tuning was done in the following areas: 1) NN architecture; 2) best augmentation parameters; 3) best CV5 seed that gives similar scores on all folds.
Take subset of NNs, with mean prediction that gives the best CV score on train data.
Group mean predictions from the previous step by incidence angle (train and test data together). For each group calculate the following features: mean prediction, median prediction, total number of samples in a group. During this calculation original train labels can be used to boost precision even further, as long as they don't propagate to the sample predictions itself.
Run KNN regressor on predictions from step 2) and incidence angle.
Train LightGBM model on the features from the steps 2), 3) and 4) (only 5 features in total).
Fine tune LightGBM using CV on train data.
Clip final probabilities towards interval (0.001, 0.999), mainly as a precaution.
Additional notes:
we ended up using a simple NN architecture from this paper:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1612.00983.pdf
It's important to skip incidence angle while training NNs in step 1), so that they can prioritize image features.
It's important to calculate group features in step 3) on both train + test data, to avoid overfitting towards train data distribution.
it's important to do a proper CV at every step any parameters are tuned in the algorithm.
the fact that images with similar incident angle have similar object class on them is exploited by LightGBM in step 6), based on features in step 3).
Looking forward to see other solutions!

solutions.2nd place:
Hi, an honor to compete with you all! I really learned a lot from doing this competition and from everyone here, and congrats to Heng CherKeng, Ryan Sun, and See!
I thought I'd share my methodology, with a focus on parts I haven't seen discussed here yet.
I was able to get a 90.9% private LB on a single model, but wasn't able to fully benefit from ensembling (I'm not very experienced in that, but learned a lot in a short time from the forums here). My ensembling technique was to vary a few parameters from the main model and average the square roots of the models' probabilities.
Model Architecture:
I used 120 log-mel filterbanks for my best model. Given this, I thought it was important to create a model that treated time and frequency differently. Specifically, I didn't do any downsampling in the time domain until the very end. With time as the first dimension and frequency as the second, my model architecture was:
1) Conv2d(64, [7,3] )
I thought of this as a "denoising" and basic feature extraction step
2) MaxPool( [1,3] )
Getting back down to the standard 40 frequency features
3) Conv2d(128, [1,7] )
Look for local patterns across frequency bands
4) MaxPool( [1,4] )
Allow for speaker variation, similar to what worked here:
https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1186%2Fs13636-015-0068-3.pdf
5) Conv2d(256 [1,10], padding="VALID")
This allows it to treat each remaining freq band very differently, and compress the frequency dimension entirely. I think of this as detecting phoneme-level features
6) Conv2d(512,[7,1])
I think of this as looking for connected components of a short keyword at different points in time
7) GlobalMaxPool in time
Collect all the components
8) Dropout + Fully Connected 256
Because why not, and seemed to work well
Data Augmentation/Standardization:
In addition to time stretching (which gave a boost of +1% LB), there were two techniques I applied that I haven't seen mentioned yet here that I think really helped.
1) Standardize Peak (Windowed) Volume
Basically, I took every clip, split it into 20 to 50 chunks, and then standardized the volume of the clips so that every clip had the same max chunk volume. Why this approach? Well, standardizing by average volume would be fine, but since some keywords were longer than others, very short . keywords would have a low average volume even though the part of the WAV containing the actual word could be quite loud.
When I implemented this, my LB score went from 82% to 84%
My theory is that by doing this, the convnet didn't have to deal with as many issues in terms of different scales for the same feature, since the volumes of the WAVs spanned orders or magnitude. Obviously using Log Mels helped with this too.
2) Vocal Tract Length Perturbation
I used VTLP as described in this paper
https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/3de0/616eb3cd4554fdf9fd65c9c82f2605a17413.pdf
This perturbation could be applied when creating the weight matrix to convert a spectrogram into log mels, so it was a very fast augmentation method
This increased my LB score +1%, and I saw the greatest benefit using the same VTLP factor within a batch, along the line of reasoning described here:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00722
solutions.3rd place:
I got sometime today to clean up my code and write the solution doc.
Pushed them here
https://github.com/xiaozhouwang/tensorflow_speech_recognition_solution
My best single model was only 0.87 on public LB and ensemble of them could only barely enter 0.89. The boost came from two semi supervised learning techniques. You can refer to the code and doc but I also conveniently posted the key part below:
Models
10 main models were trained
Resnet with 9 layers on mfcc and mel (input reshaped to 128 * 128)
Senet18 on mfcc and mel (input reshaped to 128 * 128)
Densenet121 on mfcc and mel (input reshaped to 128 * 128)
VGG (with GlobalMaxPooling+GlobalAveragePooling in the end) on mfcc and mel (input reshaped to 128 * 128)
VGG (with GlobalMaxPooling+GlobalAveragePooling in the end) on raw input
VGG (with fully connected layers in the end) on mel where it only convs along the time axis
Semi Supervised Learning
Weighted average of previously trained 10 models was used as the “ground truth” labels for test data. Two semi supervised learning techniques were used:
100% of training data + 20%-35% of test data selected per epoch were used as the new training data. Resnet (mfcc and mel), Senet (mfcc and mel) and VGG (mel and raw) were trained this way.
100% of test data were used to train a “pretrained” model. And then the weights of the “pretrained” model were loaded as initial weights to train the same model with only training data (fine tuning with training data). It turned out that fine tuning with only one epoch was enough to “correct” the overfitted “pretrained” model.
Both techniques were used with the hope that they could learn/approximate the test distribution better (instead of “overfitting” training data distribution). First one does it on the data level and second one does it on the model level.
Thank you Kaggle and Google Brain team for this great competition and congrats to all top teams! This surely wasn't an easy competition and I had quite a lot of fun doing it!
